documents.title: Introduction to Applied Dental Biomaterial (Practical)
documents.description: Practical orientation to the restorative workflow — examination, diagnosis, planning and material selection, then application of materials such as amalgam, composite and glass ionomer.

documents.title: Model & Die Materials (Practical)
documents.description: Practical handling of gypsum products — calcination, the different gypsum types (plaster, dental stone, die stone) and their manufacturing, properties and uses.

documents.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials (Practical)
documents.description: Step-by-step manipulation of resin composite — pulpal protection, acid etching and bonding to enamel, adhesive application and the incremental placement technique.

documents.title: Denture Base Materials (Practical)
documents.description: Practical manipulation of heat-cured PMMA denture base — powder/liquid ratio, mixing stages, packing and processing steps for constructing a complete denture.

documents.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
documents.description: Composition, classification and physical properties of dental waxes — natural and synthetic components, thermal behaviour and their clinical and laboratory uses.

documents.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
documents.description: Investment materials used to make a mould for casting — from the wax pattern and sprue through the crucible former, ring and investment, illustrated step by step.

documents.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
documents.description: Casting machines and technique — air-pressure and centrifugal casting machines, the role of fluxes, and how the molten alloy is forced into the mould.

documents.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
documents.description: The lost-wax casting workflow in practice — making the wax pattern, spruing, investing, burnout, casting, devesting and finishing an alloy restoration.

documents.title: MCQ — Restorative & Composite Materials
documents.description: Multiple-choice question set covering dental composite fillers, resin matrix monomers, cements, pulp capping and related restorative topics — ideal for quick self-testing.

documents.title: MCQ — Gypsum, Casting & Materials
documents.description: Multiple-choice questions on gypsum chemistry, accelerators and retarders, the wax pattern and sprue, setting reactions and dental ceramics — broad practical-course revision.

documents.title: Short Questions — Impression Materials
documents.description: Fill-in-the-blank and short-answer questions on impression materials — working and setting time, elastic properties, dimensional stability, flow and hydrophilicity.

documents.title: Introduction to Impression Materials
documents.description: Definition, purpose and classification of impression materials — how a plastic material records the form and dimensions of oral tissues to produce an accurate cast.

documents.title: Elastic Impression Materials
documents.description: The elastic impression material family — hydrocolloids (agar, alginate) and elastomers — with their setting mechanisms and clinical classification.

documents.title: Elastic Impression Materials II — Elastomers
documents.description: Detailed study of elastomeric impression materials: polysulfide, condensation silicone, addition silicone and polyether — composition, setting and properties.

documents.title: Rigid Impression Materials
documents.description: Rigid (inelastic) impression materials — impression compound and zinc oxide–eugenol — including presentation, softening technique and clinical handling.

documents.title: Model & Die Materials
documents.description: Gypsum and epoxy model & die materials — definitions of impression, cast and die, plus the ideal requirements of a good model material.

documents.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
documents.description: How dental ceramic restorations are formed — stacking, infusing, pressing and machining — and the role of condensation and the green state.

documents.title: Casting Technology
documents.description: The lost-wax casting process for converting a wax pattern into an alloy restoration — spruing, investing, burnout, casting, devesting and finishing.

documents.title: Introduction to Ceramics
documents.description: Fundamentals of ceramics — compounds of metallic and non-metallic elements, crystalline vs. amorphous (glass) structures and ionic bonding.

documents.title: Dental Ceramics II — Classification
documents.description: Classification of dental ceramics by application and fabrication method — metal-ceramic and all-ceramic systems for crowns, inlays, veneers and FDPs.

documents.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
documents.description: Mechanical properties of dental ceramics — flexural strength and fracture toughness across zirconia, lithium disilicate, leucite-reinforced and feldspathic ceramics.

documents.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
documents.description: Composition and behaviour of resin composites — organic matrix, inorganic fillers, coupling agent and initiator-activator system used as an esthetic restorative material.

documents.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
documents.description: Applications and ideal requirements of dental cements — cavity lining, luting of crowns and bridges, temporary and permanent fillings, and biological properties.

documents.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
documents.description: Glass ionomer cement in depth — water-based chemistry, modes of supply (powder/liquid, water-settable, capsules, paste-paste) with advantages and disadvantages.

documents.title: Polymer Denture Base Materials & Soft Liners
documents.description: Polymerisation chemistry and PMMA denture base materials — addition vs. condensation reactions, residual monomer, and soft liner materials.

documents.title: Dental Casting Alloys
documents.description: Classification of dental casting alloys by nobility (high-noble, noble, base metal) and by mechanical type (I–IV) for inlays, onlays, crowns and bridge/RPD frameworks.

documents.title: Level 2 Instruments — Illustrated Reference Kit
documents.description: The complete illustrated instrument and materials reference for Removable Prosthodontics & Occlusion, organised into 10 categories with required and recommended items clearly marked.

documents.title: Operative & Fixed Prosthodontics — Instruments
documents.description: Instrument and material list covering operative dentistry burs and diagnostic set plus the Fixed Prosthodontics Tech-I diamond stones and handpieces.

documents.title: Odontogenesis — Development & Growth of Teeth
documents.description: The foundation of tooth development — intra-uterine phases, the three germ layers and the crucial role of neural crest cells in forming dentin, pulp, cementum and the PDL.

documents.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
documents.description: Histological features of the cap stage — the enamel organ (outer & inner dental epithelia, stellate reticulum, enamel knot & cord), the dental papilla and the dental sac.

documents.title: Root Formation & Hertwig's Epithelial Root Sheath
documents.description: How the root forms once the crown is complete — the epithelial diaphragm and Hertwig's epithelial root sheath (ERSH) that molds the shape of the root.

documents.title: Enamel — Introduction
documents.description: Introducing enamel — the hardest, most highly mineralised tissue in the body, its ectodermal origin, the DEJ and CEJ, and why it cannot be regenerated once lost.

documents.title: Enamel — Chemical Composition & Proteins
documents.description: The composition of enamel — inorganic, organic and water content — and the unique non-collagenous matrix proteins: amelogenins and non-amelogenins (enamelin, ameloblastin).

documents.title: Enamel — Hunter-Schreger Bands
documents.description: The optical phenomenon of Hunter-Schreger bands — alternating dark and light zones seen in a ground section, arising from the changing direction of enamel rods.

documents.title: Enamel — Histological Structures
documents.description: The histological landmarks of enamel — the dentinoenamel junction (DEJ), incremental lines, enamel lamellae, enamel tufts and enamel spindles.

documents.title: Enamel — Tufts, Lamellae & Spindles
documents.description: A closer look at enamel tufts, lamellae and spindles, the neonatal line and the trapped odontoblastic processes — plus their clinical relevance to caries spread.

documents.title: Life History of Ameloblasts
documents.description: The seven stages of the ameloblast life cycle — morphogenetic, differentiating, secretory, transitional, maturative, protective and desmolytic — from the early bell stage.

documents.title: Amelogenesis — Matrix Formation & Mineralization
documents.description: How enamel is formed — organic matrix formation and mineralization, the rodless and rod (prismatic) enamel layers, Tomes' processes and the maturation stages.

documents.title: Dentin
documents.description: The main bulk of the tooth — physical and chemical characteristics of dentin, its collagen and hydroxyapatite content, and how it is studied in ground and decalcified sections.

documents.title: Dental Pulp
documents.description: The soft, richly vascularised and innervated connective tissue at the centre of the tooth — the pulp chamber, root canals, pulp horns, apical foramen and accessory canals.

documents.title: Periodontium & Periodontal Ligament
documents.description: The tooth's supporting apparatus — cementum, periodontal ligament, alveolar bone and gingiva — forming the specialised fibrous joint (gomphosis), plus the PDL's width and development.

documents.title: Periodontal Ligament — Histological Structure
documents.description: The histological components of the periodontal ligament — its cells (fibroblasts, osteoblasts, cementoblasts, defensive & progenitor cells), fibers, ground substance and interstitial tissue.

documents.title: Cementum
documents.description: The specialised calcified tissue covering the anatomical root — its development from cementoblasts, physical characteristics, chemical composition and role in attaching Sharpey's fibers.

documents.title: Alveolar Bone
documents.description: The specialised hard connective tissue lining the tooth socket — its chemical composition, functions, and the hormonal, mechanical and cytokine factors that regulate bone physiology.

documents.title: Removable Prosthodontics & Occlusion — Instrument List
documents.description: Quick-reference instrument and material checklist for the removable prosthodontics and occlusion lab, including the PKT kit, waxes, casts and mean-value articulator.

chunks.title: Model & Die Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Manipulation
chunks.text:
Manipulation
 Be sure that the bowl and spatula should be clean.
Remnants from previous mixing accelerate the setting
reaction by acting as nuclei of crystallization.
 N.B. Gypsum products powder should be protected from
moisture contamination.
 During storage because moisture contamination may
change some hemihydrate particles into dihydrate. This
will increase the number of nuclei of crystallization
leading to decrease in the setting time.
 But, after a while more and more dihydrate is formed
leading to reverse effect and increase in setting time.

 The safest method for soaking the cast is to place
the cast in a water bath with gypsum debris
remaining material located at the bottom of the
container (saturated solution of calcium
sulphate).

chunks.title: Model & Die Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Disinfection or Infection control
chunks.text:
Disinfection or Infection control
 Models can be disinfected by immersion in 1:10 dilution of
sodium hypochlorite to prevent cross contamination to the
dental office personnel by micro-organisms including
Hepatitis B Virus and Human Immuno deficiency
Virus(HIV).

chunks.title: Model & Die Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Uses
chunks.text:
Uses
Depending on the properties of each product, they have different
uses.

1. Impression plaster "Type I":
Rarely used nowadays as it is anelastic, has low mechanical properties
and its setting reaction is exothermic. Used for mounting articulators,
and for final impression.

2. Model plaster "Type II":
Used when mechanical properties are not of prime importance as in
primary casts. It is used principally for primary casts or study casts.

3. Dental stone "Type III":
Used for construction of secondary casts e.g. casts used in the
fabrication of full dentures.

chunks.title: Model & Die Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Uses
chunks.text:
Uses
6.4. High strength stone "Type IV" or die stone:
It is stronger ,harder and denser, therefore, used for the
construction of harder and stronger models and single dies
(figure 11c). Characterized by slight expansion.
6.5. High strength/high expansion stone "Type V":
The improved strength is attained by lowering the W/P ratio
even more than Type IV stone.
In addition, the setting expansion has been increased.
It is used when higher die expansion is needed to
compensate for the solidification shrinkage of new base
metal alloys having greater casting shrinkage.
Can not be used for fabrication of inlay or onlay.

4. Forming micro-pores that are penetrated by
adhesive to form resin tags.

chunks.heading: Manipulation of heat-cured PMMA
chunks.text:
Manipulation of heat-cured PMMA
I-General instructions

The majority of PMMA formulations are supplied as polymeric powders and
colorless monomer liquids.

The exothermic chemical reaction starts upon mixing of the PMMA powder and
liquid

To avoid any errors , it is necessary to use the recommended ratio of PMMA
powder and liquid (usually 3–3.5:1 v/v).

In the case of a high powder-to-liquid ratio, this means that not all of the PMMA
beads will be wet, leading to a granular texture

while a low powder-to-liquid ratio enhances polymerization shrinkage and
dimensional changes

chunks.title: Denture Base Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: II-Stages of manipulation
chunks.text:
II-Stages of manipulation
Depending on the consistency: the manipulation of PMMA mixing can be divided
into distinct stages (such as sandy, stringy, doughy, rubbery, and stiff stages), which
are followed by packing and finishing of denture bases

Sandy The mixing process starts with the sandy stage:, giving the mixture a grainy appearance.
There is hardly any chemically interaction or polymerization during this stage

In the stringy stage, the monomer molecules attack and dissolve PMMA particles.
Stringy

characterized by formation of sticky strings upon touching or stretching

chunks.title: Denture Base Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Dough stage is characterized by the loss of stringiness and stickiness
chunks.text:
Dough stage is characterized by the loss of stringiness and stickiness
Dough
.

the mixture is considered suitable for packing into a dental flask.

rubbery The doughy stage progress to the rubbery stage by further conversion of monomers into
polymers and evaporation of the residual monomers.

rubbery appearance of the matrix (which rebounds after releasing compressive or tensile
stresses)

Unable to be packed into the compression molds

IV-Compression molding packing
method
• - the PMMA in the dough stage is packed into
specialized dental flasks under compression.
• -Due to the method’s accuracy and low cost,
compression molding is frequently used for making
heat-cured PMMA prostheses .
• -The dental flask packed with PMMA is heated in a
water bath under the defined time and temperature
conditions (look at table of heat cycles).
• -the temperature of the water bath should be
increased gradually.

• Immersion of the dental flask directly into boiling
water results in evaporation of the monomer (boiling
point 100.3 C) before polymerization and increasing
porosity in the cured material

denture flask and its contents

as solids or as liquids.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • 1-Melting range & Thermal properties:
chunks.text:
• 1-Melting range & Thermal properties:
• 1- No definite melting point, because they are a mixture of different
components
• 2- Waxes have melting range
• 3-At the low end of the range, some but not all of the components
melt, which causes the wax (still solid) to flow much more.
• 4-As the temperature increases through the melting range, more of the
components melt and the wax flows more and more, then all
components become a liquid.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Solid-solid transition temperature is the temperature below melting
chunks.text:
• Solid-solid transition temperature is the temperature below melting
range

• Wax at solid-solid transition temperature will acquire flow and ductile
properties

• You can manipulate and carve wax at solid-solid temperature
satisfactory without flaking or tearing

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • 2-Excess Residue:
chunks.text:
• 2-Excess Residue:
• Because wax patterns used in the lost-wax technique are melted or burned or
ignited to remove them from the casting mold, the wax must not leave a
residue or remnants, which can affect the quality of the final restoration.

Lost-wax technique.

https://pocketdentistry.com/10-waxes/

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: 3-Flow:
chunks.text:
3-Flow:
Flow is the change in shape under an applied force.

It is caused by the slippage of the long-chained wax molecules over each other.

Flow is highly dependent on temperature and time.

At low temperatures, waxes nearly do not flow at all, but as the temperature
approaches the melting range of the wax, the flow increases dramatically

For pattern waxes, flow is generally not required at room or mouth temperature,
because it results in a permanent distortion of the wax pattern.

For boxing and utility processing waxes, flow is a highly desirable property because
these waxes need to be pliable at room temperature.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: Flow of wax.
chunks.text:
Flow of wax.

Flow is a function of time and temperature.

If a small weight, W, is placed on top of a cylindrical wax
sample (shaded area), no change in height occurs if the
wax is at a low temperature relative to its flow
temperature (top row).

As the temperature approaches the flow temperature,
some change in dimension occurs over time, medium
temperature (second row).

At the flow temperature, large changes in dimension
occur, flow temperature (bottom row).

In all cases, the amount of flow is time dependent and
usually is expressed as a percentage of the original height.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Flow = plastic deformation = Time, force and temperature dependent
chunks.text:
• Flow = plastic deformation = Time, force and temperature dependent
• Flow is low at temp. under solid-solid transition temperature
• It increases as temperature increases above transition temperature
• Flow gives wax ductile properties
• Wax ductility increases as temperature increases
• You should manipulate wax (carving , shaping etc….) in the solid-solid
transition temperature not higher as the wax will be molten not lower
as the wax would be too hard and will be liable to flake and cracking.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • 4-Thermal Expansion:
chunks.text:
• 4-Thermal Expansion:

• When waxes are heated, they expand significantly.
• This expansion can be quantified as a percentage of the original
dimension of the specimen
• In general, waxes have the highest coefficients of thermal expansion of
any dental material
• In pattern waxes, the thermal expansion is so critical, as small changes
in temperature can cause sufficient changes in dimensions to make
the pattern inaccurate.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Thermal expansion of wax.
chunks.text:
• Thermal expansion of wax.

• As wax is heated, a significant
expansion takes place but may not be
linear with the increase in
temperature.

• As the wax cools, contraction occurs
but not reversibly.

So, a wax pattern that goes through a
heating-and-cooling cycle may have
distorted dimensions

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • 5-Residual Stress:
chunks.text:
• 5-Residual Stress:
• Residual stress is the stress remaining in wax as a result of
manipulation during heating, cooling, bending, carving, or
other manipulations.

• Manipulation of wax puts molecules of the wax into positions
that they hate but cannot change because of their solid state,
causing generation of residual stresses.

• These stresses are released as the temperature of the wax
increases, and the wax molecules can move more freely.

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: Residual stresses
chunks.text:
Residual stresses
• A pattern wax is used to create a
model of a dental restoration
that will be cast using the lost-
wax technique
• The release of residual stresses
at higher temperatures causes
an irreversible changes and
deformation that can destroy
the accuracy and fit of a wax
pattern.
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/215935405_Waxing_Techniques_to_Devel
op_Proper_Occlusal_Morphology_in_Different_Occlusal_Schemes/figures

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • HOW to overcome this problem?:
chunks.text:
• HOW to overcome this problem?:
• 1- preventing residual stresses from forming :waxes should not be carved or
burnished at cold temperatures below their solid-solid transition
temperature. So Wax patterns are carved with warm instruments, and
melted wax is added in small increments (increment by increment) to
prevent rapid sudden or uneven cooling, to prevent residual stress.
• 2- To prevent the release of stress already created: A-wax should not be
subjected to temperature changes and not to be stored at high temperatures
• B - The time between finishing and investing the pattern should be
minimized (about 10 minutes) because longer storage times allow time for
release of stresses

chunks.heading: I- PATTERN WAXES

I- PATTERN WAXES
• Pattern waxes are used to create a model of a dental restoration such

chunks.title: Dental Wax (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Important Properties of Pattern Waxes
chunks.text:
• Important Properties of Pattern Waxes
• 1-All pattern waxes must have low flow at their working temperature (e.g. room
temperature) to prevent deformation of the wax pattern.
• 2-The melting range of the wax must be higher than the environment in which the
pattern is made.
- 3-On the other hand, too high melting range is undesirable as it may cause
development of residual stresses.

• 4-Finally, all pattern waxes must burn out with no residue because the residue would
interfere with the casting of the pattern.

METAL OR ALLOY IS CAST.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: IDEAL REQUIREMENTS:
chunks.text:
IDEAL REQUIREMENTS:

1) SHOULD WITHSTAND HIGH TEMPERATURE WITHOUT DECOMPOSITION DURING CASTING.
2) SHOULD HAVE SUFFICIENT EXPANSION TO COMPENSATE FOR THE CASTING SHRINKAGE.
3) SHOULD HAVE SUFFICIENT STRENGTH AT;
- ROOM TEMPERATURE, TO WITHSTAND MANIPULATION WITHOUT FRACTURE.
- HIGH TEMPERATURE, TO WITHSTAND THE FORCE OF MOLTEN ALLOY ENTERING THE MOLD.
4) SHOULD BE POROUS TO ALLOW ESCAPE OF AIR OR GASES DURING CASTING.
5) SHOULD PRODUCE A SMOOTH SURFACE AND FINE DETAILS OF THE CASTING.
6) SHOULD BE BROKEN AWAY EASILY AFTER CASTING.

1- REFRACTORY MATERIAL 65% :
PROPERTIES OF SILICA ‘ALLOTROPY OR
POLYMORPHISM’
POLYMORPHISM IS THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE CHEMICAL
COMPOUND FROM ONE CRYSTAL STRUCTURE TO ANOTHER

COMPOSITION: WITHOUT A CHANGE IN THE CHEMICAL COMPOSITION.
SILICA IS A POLYMORPHIC MATERIAL.
IT EXISTS IN FOUR DIFFERENT ALLOTROPIC
FORMS: QUARTZ, TRIDYMITE, CRISTOBALITE, AND
FUSED QUARTZ.

ALL FORMS ARE CHEMICALLY THE SAME (SIO2) BUT DIFFER
IN THE CRYSTAL STRUCTURE AND, THEREFORE, HAVE
DIFFERENT PHYSICAL PROPERTIES.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Gypsum Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Gypsum Bonded Investment
Composition:
A. Refractory material: Silica mainly in the form of cristobalite to provide
thermal expansion of the mold (small amounts of quartz may be present).

A. Binder: -calcium sulfate hemihydrate known as dental stone. It
providesboth strength and porosity.

A. Additives: Chemicals and modif iers such as:
 Charcoal or graphite is added to reduce any oxides formed on the
metal (act as reducing agents).
 Boric acid is added to:
a. Eliminate the contraction caused by gypsum when it is heated above300 °C.
b. Regulate the setting time and setting expansion.
 Coloring agents are also added.

Setting reaction:
CaSO4.½H2O + 1½H2O  CaSO4. 2H2O + heat

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Gypsum Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Gypsum Bonded Investment
Properties:
A. Dimensional changes:
1. Setting expansion:
Expansion occurs by outward thrusting action of the growing crystals of
gypsum.
2. Hygroscopic expansion:
It is obtained by allowing the gypsum to set under water at the initial
setting time. Excess water present between the particles will allow a space for
additional crystal growth causing the expansion.

3. Thermal expansion:
It is due to the displacive transformation of silica.
4. Shrinkage on heating:
- This may be due to the dehydration of gypsum
- This shrinkage is eliminated by small quantity of additives such as NaCl or boric
acid.
- Above 700 °C, contraction occurs due to the decomposition of CaSO4 leading to
evaporation of sulphur gases causing shrinkage, oxidation, contamination and
corrosion of the cast. Therefore, it should not be heated at temperatures above
700 °C during wax elimination.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: ** Heating from 200- 400ºC it contracts due to
chunks.text:
** Heating from 200- 400ºC it contracts due to
EFFECT OF the dehydration of the binder. This can be
eliminated by addition of chemicals (boric acid).

GYPSUM transformation of the α form to the form of
BONDED silica.

INVESTMENT

the investment leading to evolution of sulfur
trioxide gas (SO3) → shrinkage, oxidation,
contamination and corrosion of the cast.

** Above 1200°C, during melting of high fusing
dental alloys (base metal) such as nickel chromium
and cobalt chromium alloys, this will lead to

chunks.heading: Gypsum Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Gypsum Bonded Investment
Properties:
B. Strength:
It has high strength to withstand the driving force of the alloy during
casting. After cooling of the investment to room temperature, its strength
decreases because of the ﬁne cracks formed during cooling.

C. Porosity:
It is suff iciently porous to allow escape of air from the mold and prevent
back pressure porosity which can affect the f inal restoration. Uniform particle
size allows more porosity.

D. Fineness:
The investment that contains f iner particles of silica and calcium sulfate
hemihydrate, gives a smoother surface of the ﬁnished casting.

chunks.heading: Phosphate Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Phosphate Bonded Investment
Composition:
A. Refractory material: Silica mainly in the form of cristobalite to provide
thermal expansion of the mold (small amounts of quartz may be present).

A. Binder: Magnesium ammonium phosphate.

A. Additives: Chemicals and modif iers such as:
 Carbon is added as a modiﬁer to produce clean casting for gold
alloys but for silver and base metal alloys it may cause brittleness
of the alloys.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Phosphate Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Phosphate Bonded Investment
Composition:
Setting reaction:
• Magnesium ammonium phosphate results from the reaction of mono-amonium
phosphate and magnesium oxide.
• The crystals of magnesium ammonium phosphate bind together the particles of
silica (refractory materials).
• The ammonium phosphate is used in great amount so that the excess can react
with silica at an elevated temperature giving a complex that increases the
strength of the investment.
• Such an investment is mixed either with water or special liquid (silica sol)
supplied by the manufacturer.

• Silica sol is used when more expansion and/or higher temperature
resistance is required.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Phosphate Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Phosphate Bonded Investment
Properties:
A. Dimensional changes:
1. Setting expansion:
The setting reaction is accompanied by expansion similar to crystal growth
in gypsum. Higher setting expansion occurs when the investment is mixed with
silica sol.
2. Hygroscopic expansion:
Such expansion occurs when the investment is mixed with silica sol while if it
is mixed with water, the hygroscopic expansion is negligible.

3. Thermal expansion:
It is due to the displacive transformation of silica.
4. Shrinkage on heating:
- Thermal shrinkage occurs due to the decomposition of the binder and evolution of
ammonia.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Phosphate Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Phosphate Bonded Investment
Properties:
B. Strength:
Strength is high due to the reaction of silica and binder to give silica
phosphate complex. The use of silica sol instead of water increases the strength.

C. Porosity:
It is suff iciently porous to allow escape of air from the mold and prevent
back pressure porosity which can affect the f in al restoration .(Similar to
gypsum bonded investment).

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: APPLICATIONS:
chunks.text:
APPLICATIONS:
Phosphate bonded investment withstands high
temperature (1000 °C - 1100 °C).

It can be used with base metal alloys or gold
alloys.

When mixed with water it is suitable for casting gold
alloys. Carbon is added as a modiﬁer to produce
clean casting for gold alloys.

When mixed with silica sol it is suitable for casting
base metal alloys which have high melting
temperature and high casting contraction. However,
carbon should not be used for base metal alloys as it
may cause brittleness of the alloys. Thus, carbon-
free investment should be used.

B. Binder: Polysalicic acid.

chunks.title: Investment Materials (Practical)
chunks.heading: Silicate Bonded Investment
chunks.text:
Silicate Bonded Investment
Composition:
Setting reaction:
Hydrolysis:
Hydrolysis of ethyl silicate or sodium silicate in presence of hydrochloricacid
into salisic acid sol and ethyl alcohol.

Si (OC2 H 5 ) 4 + H 2 O  Si (OH) 4 + C2 H 5 OH
Ethyl silicate salicic acid sol

Gelation:
Salicic acid sol binds the crystals of cristobalite or quartz, and then it
accumulates to form polysalicic acid gel. This gelation is accompanied by
shrinkage (setting shrinkage).

Dryness:
On heating there is loss of alcohol and water leaving a mold made of silica
particles tightly packed together.

d) Thermal expansion which is usually suff icient to compensate

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: Casting
chunks.text:
Casting
• A) Air Pressure casting machine
• The precious and semi precious alloys are melted over the ring
at the top of the crucible using a torch to melt the alloy.
• Compressed air is used to force the molten alloy into the mold.

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: • B-Centrifugal casting machines:
chunks.text:
• B-Centrifugal casting machines:
• Most casting of alloys is made in a centrifugal casting machine.

• Centrifugal casting machines operate on the physical principle of
centrifugal force, in which the molten material is accelerated outward by
rapid spinning.

• The casting machine is driven with a spring or electric motor.

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: • FLUXES:
chunks.text:
• FLUXES:
• The casting alloy is heated in a crucible made of a heat-resistant ceramic .

• A flux is usually added to minimize the formation of oxides , because oxides
hinder the heating and casting of the alloy and decrease the final quality of
the casting.

• The type of flux :used depends on the temperature of casting, the type of
heat source, the type of casting alloy, and the type of investment.
• may be in case of some precious alloys made from equal parts of fused
borax powder ground with boric acid powder. The boric acid aids in retaining
the borax on the surface of the alloy.

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: • When the alloy is completely molten, the casting
chunks.text:
• When the alloy is completely molten, the casting
ring is removed from the burn out oven and is
placed behind the crucible and the crucible–ring
assembly is spun rapidly.
• Spinning accelerates the alloy into the casting ring
and into the space previously occupied by the sprue
and wax pattern.
• Casting alloys may be heated by blowtorch or
electric current.
• The most common method for heating low-
temperature alloys (<1200° C) is by blowtorch
• An electric current is used for higher temperatures
alloys, using a process called induction casting

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: • the proper heating of the alloy is critical to a successful casting:
chunks.text:
• the proper heating of the alloy is critical to a successful casting:
• If heated too little, the alloy will be too viscous to flow into all of the finest
details of the casting ring mold.
• If heated too much, the alloy may be damaged by the oxidation of
elements, or the investment may crack from the thermal shock
• The torch flame is generated from a gas mixture of propane and air, natural
gas and air, acetylene and air, or acetylene and oxygen.

Phillip’s science of dental
materials ed. 13 ch.14

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: Parts of the blowtorch flame:
chunks.text:
Parts of the blowtorch flame:

1) Mixing Zone – First zone coming out from
the nozzle . Mixing of air & gas takes place
here before combustion. No Color . No heat .

2) Combustion Zone – Second zone covering
the first one. Partial Combustion of air & gas
takes place here. Green in Color . Zone is
oxidizing & should always be kept away from
molten alloy during fusion.

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: 3) Reducing Zone – Third zone located beyond the
chunks.text:
3) Reducing Zone – Third zone located beyond the
tip of the combustion zone. Light blue in Color. It
is the hottest part of the flame . This area should
be kept constantly on the metal during melting.

4) Oxidizing Zone– Outer zone in which complete
combustion occurs with oxygen & air. Not used to
melt the alloy. Its temperature is lower than the
reducing zone & also oxidizes the alloy.

chunks.title: Casting Machines (Practical)
chunks.heading: Cooling:
chunks.text:
Cooling:

After casting, cooling is either by allowing casting ring to cool slowly
on top of a bench or is submerged immediately in cold water.

For some gold-based alloys, bench cooling produces a harder, stronger state of the alloy,
and rapid cooling in water (also called quenching) produces a softer condition.

However, many types of alloys do not obey this principle.

You choose type of cooling according to the desired mechanical
properties

chunks.heading: Centrifugal force from the
chunks.text:
Centrifugal force from the
spinning casting machine

FIG 12-6 Schematic diagram of the alloy
casting process.
After burnout of the wax from the ring, the
ring is moved from the burnout oven to the
cradle in the casting machine (left). At this
point, the alloy has been melted with the
torch in the crucible (right), which remains
in place to maintain the molten state. As
soon as possible, the casting arm is released
and the spinning force of the casting arm
generates centrifugal force (red arrow
above) that drives the molten alloy toward
the ring.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • FIG 12-1 Sequence of steps for casting using
chunks.text:
• FIG 12-1 Sequence of steps for casting using
the lost-wax technique:
1. The wax pattern is formed on the die.
2. A sprue (generally made of wax or plastic) is added
and the wax pattern is transferred to a sprue base.
3. A ring is added and the ring is filled with investment,
surrounding the wax pattern and sprue.
4. The sprue base is removed, and the ring is placed
into a hot oven that burns away the wax pattern and
sprue.
5. Molten alloy is cast into the space formerly occupied
by the wax pattern and
6. the investment is broken away (devested).
7. The sprue is removed and the crown is polished and
ready for try-in.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: •Spruing
chunks.text:
•Spruing
• A sprue forms a channel in the investment through
which the molten alloy or ceramic passes to form
the restoration.
• Sprues often are wax but also may be plastic or
metal.
• If metal, the sprue must be removed before casting
because the metal will not burn out.
• The decision of where to place one or multiple
sprues on the wax pattern is complicated and
depends on the type of restoration, the type of
casting material, and the experience of the dentist
Phillip’s science of dental
and technician .
materials ed. 13 ch.14 • In the simplest case, a single sprue is placed on one
of the cusps of the wax pattern. In more complex
cases, multiple sprues may be placed.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • The other end of the sprue is attached to a base made of rubber (sprue base)
chunks.text:
• The other end of the sprue is attached to a base made of rubber (sprue base)
(Figures 12-1 and 12-4). The sprue is attached at the apex of the cone of the
sprue base.
• The cone would form a depression in the investment to guide the molten
alloy into the sprue hole.

- Sprue diameter and length vary depending on the type of restoration but
should be selected to ensure that the cast material solidifies last in the sprue,
and by this strategy the sprue continues to “feed” the casting as it solidifies and
shrinks.

To prevent premature freezing in the sprue channel, sprues are generally as
big in diameter and as short as possible; a reservoir is often added to the
sprue to increase the sprue mass.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: INVESTING AND BURNOUT
chunks.text:
INVESTING AND BURNOUT
• Investments:
• gypsum bonded Investments that use gypsum as a binder are used to
cast alloys for inlays, onlays, full-alloy crowns, and some Ni based
partial denture frameworks.
• Gypsum alone (without silica) cannot be used for investing because it
lacks sufficient resistance to heat.
• In gypsum bonded Investments the melting temperature of an alloy
cannot exceed 1200° C, and the burnout temperature cannot exceed
700° C or the gypsum will decompose.
• phosphate-bonded investments are used for higher melting alloys .

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Phosphate bonded investments are much stronger than gypsum
chunks.text:
• Phosphate bonded investments are much stronger than gypsum
investments and are used for ceramic–alloy restorations, all-ceramic
restorations, implant substructures, and partial denture frameworks in
which casting alloys have high melting ranges.

https://mydentaltechnologynotes.wordpress.com/2018/08/12/
casting-procedures-in-dentistry/

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: •Investing:
chunks.text:
•Investing:
• Investing the wax pattern captures all details of the wax pattern into the
investment.
- To retain the investment during setting, a casting ring is placed onto the
sprue base (Figure 12-4). The casting ring also supports the investment
during the casting.

• The ring is lined with a ceramic or paper liner to help the investment to
expand during setting and burnout.

• The liner is moistened before the investment is added to:-) prevent it from
absorbing water from the investment mix .-) Also, that helps in hygroscopic
expansion of investment.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: that permits the setting expansion of the investment can be used
chunks.text:
To allow thermal and hygroscopic expansion of investment material a split ring or flexible rubber ring
that permits the setting expansion of the investment can be used

However, the most commonly used technique to provide investment
expansion is to line the walls of the unsplit casting ring with a liner.

Traditionally, asbestos was the material of choice, but it can no longer
be used because its carcinogenic potential makes it a biohazard.

Two types of non-asbestos ring liner materials have been produced:
an aluminosilicate ceramic liner and a cellulose (paper) liner.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Before investing, the wax
chunks.text:
• Before investing, the wax
pattern is treated with a
surfactant that aids flow of the
water-based (hydrophilic)
investment material over the
water-hating (hydrophobic) wax
pattern.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Once mixed, the investment is poured slowly into
chunks.text:
• Once mixed, the investment is poured slowly into
the casting ring, taking extreme care to flow the
investment around the wax pattern without
forming bubbles or voids (vibrator is used)

• Pouring till ring is full
• Vacuum mixer of investment can be used for
vacuum investing
• Vacuum investing is better than hand investing.

• Because the wax pattern is dimensionally unstable
once removed from the die, the time taken to
invest should be less than 10 minutes.

• The invested wax pattern is allowed to set for at
least 45 minutes before burnout but should not
be allowed to desiccate.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: Burnout
chunks.text:
Burnout
• Once the investment has set (after approximately 45minutes), the
casting ring is placed into an oven to burn out the wax pattern and
sprue
• wax does not melt but combusts to allow complete removal.
• After burnout, a space remains that was occupied by the wax pattern
and sprue.
• So,The sprue space forms a channel through which the molten alloy
can flow to the space formerly occupied by the wax pattern

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: Burnout oven. The invested wax pattern (without the sprue base) is placed into an
chunks.text:
Burnout oven. The invested wax pattern (without the sprue base) is placed into an
oven
(A) to burn out the wax prior to casting. The oven maintains a temperature
compatible with the
investment used .
(Dental materials foundations and applications 11 ed)

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Burnout also cause thermal expansion of the investment.
chunks.text:
• Burnout also cause thermal expansion of the investment.
• burnout provides temperature compatibility between the hot, molten
alloy and the investment, why?:- If the molten casting material were
cast into cold investment at room temperature, the rapid change in
temperature can cause cracking to the investment.
-The relatively cold investment
also would cause the casting material to solidify prematurely (early)
before the restoration space was completely filled.

• A rule of thumb is that the melting temperature (liquidus) of an alloy
should not be more than 500° C higher than the burnout temperature.

chunks.title: Casting Technology (Practical)
chunks.heading: • Once the casting ring and investment are heated, the ring should be
chunks.text:
• Once the casting ring and investment are heated, the ring should be
cast immediately before it cools to any degree; any delay of more
than 20 to 30 seconds will compromise the fit and quality of the cast
restoration.

- The thermal expansion of the investment is not reversible, and if the
ring cools before it is cast, either the investment will crack or the casting
will be distorted.

chunks.text:
I-Elastic impression materials
A-Hydrocolloids
What are colloids?

- Substances are called colloids when they consist of two or more phases with the units of at least one of the
phases having a dimension slightly greater than simple molecular size

- The range of size is usually recognized as being approximately 1 to 500 nm measured in maximum dimension
However, there are many variations between different references about determining the range of particle size
of the colloidal phases

- Colloid is a Heterogenous mixture with dispersed phase having particle size intermediate between true
solution and suspension

chunks.title: Elastic Impression Materials
chunks.heading: Important notes about colloids:
chunks.text:
Important notes about colloids:
1-True solution = Single phase

2-Colloid = two separate phases = Dispersed phase + Dispersion phase

3-When dispersion phase of a colloid is water it is called Hydrocolloid

4-Colloids can exist in two states sol or gel

5-Colloids can experience sol to gel or vise versa transformation under certain conditions and
this transformation could be reversible or irreversible.
6- In sol state the colloid exists as a viscous liquid

7- Gel exists as an elastic solid or semisolid or jellylike.

 Impression : A negative replica of oral structures.

 A Model or cast : A positive replica of oral tissues, prepared from an
impression .
 A Die: A positive replica of a single tooth ,prepared from an impression.

chunks.text:
Requirements of model and die materials:

1- It Should have high strength to resist breakage during use.
2- It Should have high hardness to resist scratching during use.
3- It should have good working time.
4. It should reproduce fine details of the impression.
5. It should have no dimensional changes during setting and storage.
6- It should have color matching with impression material.
7- Ease of use.
8- Cheap

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: Fabrication Techniques:
chunks.text:
Fabrication Techniques:
• One consequence of the strong ionic bonds in ceramics is that these
materials melt only at relatively high temperatures.

• Some techniques are used to form the final dental restoration including
stacking, infusing, pressing, or machining.

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: A-In stacking: the ceramic material is
chunks.text:
A-In stacking: the ceramic material is
ground into particles that are manipulated
into an approximation of the final form in
a “green” state (weak state).

The green state is achieved by a process
called condensation.

A viscous slurry of the porcelain particles in
water or water-glycerol is applied to a
substructure, using vibration to pack the
particles and
expel the liquid to the surface. Then liquid is
removed by a sorbent
tissue.

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: By alternatively vibrating the liquid to the
chunks.text:
By alternatively vibrating the liquid to the
surface and then removing it,
the particles become packed quite
tightly into the green state.

In the green state, the ceramic can be
carved and shaped into approximate
final form.

Applications: Stacking is used to 1) apply
ceramics to alloys or high-strength
ceramic substructures or 2) to fabricate
laminate veneers.
Stacking is used primarily for glassy and
glass-dominated ceramics

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: • B-Sintering:
chunks.text:
• B-Sintering:
• After forming the green state, the
ceramic is fired in a specialized oven
in a process called sintering.
• During sintering, the particles only
melt and fuse at their surfaces.
• After a short time (minutes), the
particles are cooled to room
temperature, and the fired ceramic
is formed.
• To reduce the “dead” air spaces in
the ceramic, a vacuum is often
applied in sintering.

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: • Important notes about sintering:
chunks.text:
• Important notes about sintering:
• The sintering temperature is often
referred to as the fusing temperature of
the ceramic.

• During sintering, significant shrinkage (up
to 10% linearly) occurs, for this reason, the
green state form is often made a bit larger
than final desired contours.

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: Reading only
chunks.text:
Reading only

• C-Infusion: is a fabrication method by which a porous sintered form is
infiltrated with a silica glass (Figure 14-7).
• In the initial step, a ceramic slurry is stacked onto a model of a tooth
preparation, sintered to provide an intermediate strength, and trimmed
to near-final form
• Next step, a silica glass is added and the restoration is sintered again.
• During the second sintering, the silica melts and flows into all the
capillary spaces of the initial structure.
• The infused ceramic has markedly higher strengths
• Infusion is used on a subset of crystalline-dominated ceramics

form, This process is similar to casting making all-ceramic cores from glass-

chunks.title: Fabrication Techniques of Dental Ceramics
chunks.heading: Machining
chunks.text:
Machining
E-Machining: Newer ceramics are machined into final form.

The replica of the tooth preparation is scanned into a computer, and
then a highly sophisticated program drives fine machining tools to mill
a ceramic block to the final form, usually in several minutes.

In the most advanced techniques, the shape of the tooth preparation is
captured digitally (so-called digital impression), and these data are
sent to the lab for milling

This technique is called Computer aided design & computer-aided
manufacturing (CAD-CAM)

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: • FIG 12-1 Sequence of steps for casting using
chunks.text:
• FIG 12-1 Sequence of steps for casting using
the lost-wax technique:
1. The wax pattern is formed on the die.
2. A sprue (generally made of wax or plastic) is added
and the wax pattern is transferred to a sprue base.
3. A ring is added and the ring is filled with investment,
surrounding the wax pattern and sprue.
4. The sprue base is removed, and the ring is placed
into a hot oven that burns away the wax pattern and
sprue.
5. Molten alloy is cast into the space formerly occupied
by the wax pattern and
6. the investment is broken away (devested).
7. The sprue is removed and the crown is polished and
ready for try-in.

chunks.heading: •Spruing
chunks.text:
•Spruing
• A sprue forms a channel in the investment through
which the molten alloy or ceramic passes to form
the restoration.
• Sprues often are wax but also may be plastic or
metal.
• If metal, the sprue must be removed before casting
because the metal will not burn out.
• The decision of where to place one or multiple
sprues on the wax pattern is complicated and
depends on the type of restoration, the type of
casting material, and the experience of the dentist
Phillip’s science of dental
and technician .
materials ed. 13 ch.14 • In the simplest case, a single sprue is placed on one

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: • The other end of the sprue is attached to a base made of rubber (sprue base)
chunks.text:
• The other end of the sprue is attached to a base made of rubber (sprue base)
(Figures 12-1 and 12-4). The sprue is attached at the apex of the cone of the
sprue base.
• The cone would form a depression in the investment to guide the molten
alloy into the sprue hole.

- Sprue diameter and length vary depending on the type of restoration but
should be selected to ensure that the cast material solidifies last in the sprue,
and by this strategy the sprue continues to “feed” the casting as it solidifies and
shrinks.

To prevent premature freezing in the sprue channel, sprues are generally as
big in diameter and as short as possible; a reservoir is often added to the
sprue to increase the sprue mass.

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: INVESTING AND BURNOUT
chunks.text:
INVESTING AND BURNOUT
• Investments:
• gypsum bonded Investments that use gypsum as a binder are used to
cast alloys for inlays, onlays, full-alloy crowns, and some Ni based
partial denture frameworks.
• Gypsum alone (without silica) cannot be used for investing because it
lacks sufficient resistance to heat.
• In gypsum bonded Investments the melting temperature of an alloy
cannot exceed 1200° C, and the burnout temperature cannot exceed
700° C or the gypsum will decompose.
• phosphate-bonded investments are used for higher melting alloys .

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: • Phosphate bonded investments are much stronger than gypsum
chunks.text:
• Phosphate bonded investments are much stronger than gypsum
investments and are used for ceramic–alloy restorations, all-ceramic
restorations, implant substructures, and partial denture frameworks in
which casting alloys have high melting ranges.

https://mydentaltechnologynotes.wordpress.com/2018/08/12/
casting-procedures-in-dentistry/

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: •Investing:
chunks.text:
•Investing:
• Investing the wax pattern captures all details of the wax pattern into the
investment.
- To retain the investment during setting, a casting ring is placed onto the
sprue base (Figure 12-4). The casting ring also supports the investment
during the casting.

• The ring is lined with a ceramic or paper liner to help the investment to
expand during setting and burnout.

• The liner is moistened before the investment is added to:-) prevent it from
absorbing water from the investment mix .-) Also, that helps in hygroscopic
expansion of investment.

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: that permits the setting expansion of the investment can be used
chunks.text:
To allow thermal and hygroscopic expansion of investment material a split ring or flexible rubber ring
that permits the setting expansion of the investment can be used

However, the most commonly used technique to provide investment
expansion is to line the walls of the unsplit casting ring with a liner.

Traditionally, asbestos was the material of choice, but it can no longer
be used because its carcinogenic potential makes it a biohazard.

Two types of non-asbestos ring liner materials have been produced:
an aluminosilicate ceramic liner and a cellulose (paper) liner.

chunks.heading: • Before investing, the wax

chunks.heading: • Once mixed, the investment is poured slowly into
chunks.text:

the casting ring, taking extreme care to flow the
investment around the wax pattern without
forming bubbles or voids (vibrator is used)

• Pouring till ring is full
• Vacuum mixer of investment can be used for
vacuum investing
• Vacuum investing is better than hand investing.

• Because the wax pattern is dimensionally unstable
once removed from the die, the time taken to
invest should be less than 10 minutes.

• The invested wax pattern is allowed to set for at
least 45 minutes before burnout but should not
be allowed to desiccate.

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: Burnout
chunks.text:
Burnout
• Once the investment has set (after approximately 45minutes), the
casting ring is placed into an oven to burn out the wax pattern and
sprue
• wax does not melt but combusts to allow complete removal.
• After burnout, a space remains that was occupied by the wax pattern
and sprue.
• So,The sprue space forms a channel through which the molten alloy
can flow to the space formerly occupied by the wax pattern

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: Burnout oven. The invested wax pattern (without the sprue base) is placed into an
chunks.text:
Burnout oven. The invested wax pattern (without the sprue base) is placed into an
oven
(A) to burn out the wax prior to casting. The oven maintains a temperature
compatible with the
investment used .
(Dental materials foundations and applications 11 ed)

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: • Burnout also cause thermal expansion of the investment.
chunks.text:
• Burnout also cause thermal expansion of the investment.
• burnout provides temperature compatibility between the hot, molten
alloy and the investment, why?:- If the molten casting material were
cast into cold investment at room temperature, the rapid change in
temperature can cause cracking to the investment.
-The relatively cold investment
also would cause the casting material to solidify prematurely (early)
before the restoration space was completely filled.

• A rule of thumb is that the melting temperature (liquidus) of an alloy
should not be more than 500° C higher than the burnout temperature.

chunks.title: Casting Technology
chunks.heading: • Once the casting ring and investment are heated, the ring should be
chunks.text:
• Once the casting ring and investment are heated, the ring should be
cast immediately before it cools to any degree; any delay of more
than 20 to 30 seconds will compromise the fit and quality of the cast
restoration.

- The thermal expansion of the investment is not reversible, and if the
ring cools before it is cast, either the investment will crack or the casting
will be distorted.

chunks.title: Introduction to Ceramics
chunks.heading: Basic Ideas about Ceramics in
chunks.text:
Basic Ideas about Ceramics in
Dentistry:

• At the atomic level, ceramics are
composed of metal–oxygen ionic
bonds (see Figure 14-1). Silicon (Si),
zirconium (Zr), and aluminum (Al)
are common metallic elements that
occur in ceramics in combination
with oxygen.
• Ionic bonds are strong and they do
not tolerate bending This
intolerance makes ceramics
brittle.

chunks.title: Introduction to Ceramics
chunks.heading: • A second feature of ceramics is
chunks.text:
• A second feature of ceramics is
that the metal–oxygen ionic
bonds occur in vast crystalline
arrays (see Figure 14-1B).

FIG 14-1B Ceramics are composed of arrays of metal atoms and oxygen held together by ionic
bonds. These ionic bonds result from the transfer of electrons from the metal to oxygen, and they
are strong (i.e., the bonds do not tolerate distortion). The metals and oxygen form arrays in a three-
dimensional crystalline lattice that makes up the ceramic particle..

chunks.title: Introduction to Ceramics
chunks.heading: The continuity of the array may be
chunks.text:
The continuity of the array may be
interrupted by the presence of metal ions
of sodium (Na) or potassium (K) for
example.

These interrupting ions are called fluxes.

Fluxes have several important effects on
ceramic properties, including reduced
strength, lower fusing temperature, and
more transparency

chunks.title: Introduction to Ceramics
chunks.heading: When the crystalline array is
chunks.text:
When the crystalline array is
disrupted sufficiently, it is
described as amorphous or
glassy

The ratio between crystalline
and amorphous areas in a
ceramic fundamentally
determines how the ceramic
will behave clinically in the
mouth

chunks.heading: The terms ceramic and porcelain are often used interchangeably, but
chunks.text:
The terms ceramic and porcelain are often used interchangeably, but
incorrectly.

Ceramic refers to any material composed of the arrays of metallic oxygen
bonds described previously.

on the other hand, Porcelain is a type of ceramic that results when feldspar
(K2O-Al O3-SiO2) + silica (SiO2) + and alumina (Al2O3) are fired together
2

with fluxes such as sodium carbonate (Na CO ) or potassium carbonate
2 3

(K CO )
2 3

During the firing of porcelain, large areas of amorphous ceramic are
formed, with small islands of a crystalline phase called leucite.

chunks.text:
Types and Uses of Ceramics in Dentistry Today (Figures 14-3 and 14-4).
Dental ceramics may be roughly classified into four types:
1-Traditional feldspathic (or glassy),
2- Glass dominated,
3-Crystalline dominated,
4-Crystalline
All are a consequence of the ratio of amorphous to crystalline phases and how the
phases interact with one another .

chunks.text:
Feldspathic ceramics remain among the most esthetic and weakest of
the dental ceramics and are primarily used:
1- as veneers over alloys or ceramic substructures that impart
strength to the restoration and support the weaker veneer

2- Feldspathic ceramics also are used for veneers that are bonded
directly to tooth structure, particularly in the upper anterior region

Feldspathic ceramics can not be used as a full ceramic crown

chunks.title: Introduction to Ceramics
chunks.heading: 4-The crystalline ceramics are the newest and strongest of the ceramics
chunks.text:
4-The crystalline ceramics are the newest and strongest of the ceramics
used in dentistry (see Figure 14-3).
These ceramics are formed from either alumina or zirconia that has
been seeded with other ions such as magnesium or yttrium to
optimize their properties

Crystalline ceramics have no glassy phase and are opaque.
They cannot serve as esthetic veneers on alloys.
they are used as:
1-high-strength cores, including posterior crowns and bridges,
2- and for making full ceramic posterior crowns or bridges
3- core for anterior crown or anterior bridges.
4- recently translucent zirconia is used as full contour crowns for areas
not subjected to high forces of mastication.

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics II — Classification
chunks.heading: II-Stress-induced transformation toughening
chunks.text:
II-Stress-induced transformation toughening
Stress-induced transformation toughening is obtained, for example, in ceramics consisting
of partially stabilized tetragonal zirconia

Zirconia (ZrO2) exists under different crystallographic forms.
The monoclinic form is stable at all temperatures below 1170°C.

The tetragonal form is stable between 1170° and up to 2370°C.

The transformation from the tetragonal to the monoclinic form by cooling
causes a volume increase of the unit cell.

So, pure unalloyed zirconia cannot be obtained at room temperature;
as the zirconia would shatter upon cooling due to the transformation and
volume increase WHY?
Because Tetragonal changed to higher volume monoclinic form.

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics II — Classification
chunks.heading: How to overcome this problem????
chunks.text:
How to overcome this problem????

The tetragonal form can be partially stabilized to room temperature by doping with
different oxides, such as yttrium oxide (Y2O3) or cerium oxide (CeO2).

e.g. Zirconia-based dental ceramics produced by machining followed by sintering
at high temperatures consist of : tetragonal zirconia polycrystals, partially stabilized
by 3 mole percent yttrium (3Y-TZP).

https://pocketdentistry.com/11-restorative-
materials-ceramics/

chunks.text:
Advantages of metastability of zirconia ?????????????

This partial stabilization or metastability of the tetragonal phase allows the transformation
from tetragonal to monoclinic to occur when ?? When external stresses are applied.

This transformation is stress induced and is accompanied by a volume
increase + compressive stresses at the crack tip leading to closing and
arrest of the crack in the transformed zone

Transformation toughening leads to the excellent mechanical properties
of 3Y-TZP.

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics II — Classification
chunks.heading: Glazing: is an extrinsic strengthening method and
chunks.text:
Glazing: is an extrinsic strengthening method and
is the final step in the fabrication of metal-ceramic
restorations.

- A low-expansion glass called glaze can be applied to
the surface of the ceramic, then fired to high
temperature. Upon cooling, this glaze layer is placed
under compression from the greater contraction of the
underlying ceramic.

- This layer reduces depth and width of the surface
flaws, thereby improving the overall resistance of the
ceramic to crack propagation.

C-Fracture toughness (Craig Textbook 2020)

- Fracture toughness is another important property of ceramics

- it measures the resistance to brittle fracture when a crack is present

- 3Y-TZP ceramics have the highest fracture toughness of all-ceramic
materials,

- Followed by lithium disilicate–reinforced ceramics

Then Leucite-reinforced ceramics exhibit slightly higher fracture toughness
values than feldspathic porcelain

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: D- Hardness
chunks.text:
D- Hardness
The hardness of most glassy or glass-dominated ceramics is substantially higher (>460
kg/mm2) than human enamel (343 kg/mm2), SO WHEN ceramics occlude against
natural teeth, the enamel may wear.

Ceramic-induced wear of opposing enamel may be a problem for fixed prosthetic
appliances

Newer crystalline ceramics have a hardness of 1200 to 1500 kg/mm2, so the risk of
wear of natural teeth is higher.

Current evidence suggests that ceramic-induced wear can be minimized if the
restoration surface is very smooth.

Therefore, clinical polishing is very important for these ceramic restorations
Dental material foundations and applications 11th edition

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: II-Other important physical properties
chunks.text:
II-Other important physical properties
1-coefficient of thermal expansion CTE
A ceramic with a high coefficient of thermal expansion expands a large amount when heated
and contracts a large amount when cooled.

The coefficient of thermal expansion is important when a ceramic is bonded to an alloy (ceramic–alloy
restoration) or ceramic core (all-ceramic restoration).

The expansion of the alloy or core and veneering ceramic must be
appropriately matched, or the ceramic will fracture when the restoration
cools from firing temperature to room temperature

Dental material foundations and applications 11th edition

Glassy ceramics are classified according to their fusing temperature (also called sintering temperature) as

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: III-Biological properties
chunks.text:
III-Biological properties
-Some mass loss (corrosion) of glassy ceramics occurs during service, although the
amount of mass released is low relative to polymers or alloys that are used in
restorative dentistry.

-There is debate in literature and between researchers about radioactivity hazards of
zirconia

- Acidulated phosphate fluoride (APF), one of the most commonly used fluoride gels
for caries control, is known to etch glass by selective leaching of sodium ions, thereby
disrupting the silica
network.

- Dentists should be aware of these long-term clinical effects of fluorides on ceramic
and composite restorations and avoid the use of APF gels when composites and
ceramics are present

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: Practical
chunks.text:
Practical
Requirements for a Metal-Ceramic System (Craig Textbook 2020)
1-The alloy must have a high melting temperature. The melting range must be
substantially higher (greater than 100°C) than the firing temperature of the veneering
porcelain and solders used to join segments of an FDP. (metal)

2. The veneering porcelain must have a low fusing temperature so that no creep, sag, or
distortion of the framework takes place during sintering. (ceramic)

3. The porcelain must wet the alloy when applied as a slurry to prevent voids forming
at the metal-ceramic interface. In general, the contact angle should be 60 degrees or less.
(ceramic)

4. A strong bond between the ceramic and metal is essential and is achieved by: 1-
chemical reaction of the opaque porcelain with metal oxides on the surface of metal
and by 2-mechanical interlocking made possible by roughening of the metal coping.
(ceramo-metallic)

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: Practical
chunks.text:
Practical
5. CTEs of the porcelain and metal must be compatible so that :the veneering porcelain
never undergoes tensile stresses, which would lead to cracking. Metal-ceramic systems
are therefore designed so that the CTE of the metal is slightly higher than that of the
porcelain, thus placing the veneering porcelain in compression . (ceramo-metallic)

6. Adequate stiffness and strength of the metal framework are especially important for
FDPs and posterior crowns. (metal)

7. High resistance to deformation at high temperature is essential. Metal
copings are relatively thin (0.4 to 0.5 mm); no distortion should occur during
firing of the porcelain. (metal)

8. Adequate design of the restoration is critical. The preparation should provide : 1-adequate

9-During preparation of the metal framework before porcelain application, it is important that
all sharp angles be eliminated and rounded to avoid stress concentration in the
porcelain.(preparation)

10- If full porcelain coverage is not used and a metal occlusal surface is used, the position of
the metal ceramic junction should be located at least 1.5 mm from all centric occlusal contacts.

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: Machinable All-Ceramic Materials
chunks.text:
Machinable All-Ceramic Materials
A-Ceramic materials can be machined in the fully sintered state and termed hard machining and
restorations produced in this way are machined directly to final size. So, in hard machining ceramics
are fully sintered before machining.

B-Some all-ceramic materials can also be machined in a soft, partially sintered state then later fully
sintered. This is called soft machining.

The latter technique requires milling of enlarged restorations to compensate for sintering
shrinkage as in zirconia

(Craig Textbook 2020)

chunks.title: Dental Ceramics III — Mechanical Properties
chunks.heading: Hard machining of lithium disilicate ceramics
chunks.text:
Hard machining of lithium disilicate ceramics

lithium disilicate glass-ceramic blocks are available for hard
machining by CAD/ CAM.

The lithium disilicate glass-ceramic blocks are machined in a partially
crystallized state, which corresponds to a softer and easier-to-
machine state.

After the restorations are machined, a heat treatment at 850°C for 10
minutes is performed to complete the crystallization process, and
therefore ensure that the lithium disilicate ceramic possesses
improved mechanical properties before glazing and cementation.

(Craig Textbook 2020)

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Definitions
chunks.text:
Definitions
Composite :
A combination of two or more chemically different materials
with a distinct interface between the different components.

Resin Composite:
A resin material used in dentistry as an esthetic restorative
material.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Composition
chunks.text:
Composition
1. Organic matrix.
2. Inorganic fillers.
3. Coupling agent.
4. Initiator-activator system.
5. Polymerization inhibitor.
6. Ultraviolet stabilizer.
7. Pigments.

1. Diethylene glycol dimethacrylate (DEGDMA).

1. Reduce the viscosity of the matrix ( allow incorporation of more

2. Facilitate the clinical manipulation.

2. Increase water sorption.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 2. Inorganic fillers (Dispersed Phase):
chunks.text:
2. Inorganic fillers (Dispersed Phase):
Role of Fillers:
1. Improve the mechanical properties.
2. Reduce the polymerization shrinkage.
3. Decrease the coefficient of thermal expansion and
contraction.
4. Reduce the heat evolved during polymerization .
5. Decrease water sorption.
6. Glass fillers reflect the color of the surrounding tooth
structure so increase aesthetics.
7. Barium , strontium and zirconia fillers provide radio-
opacity.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 2. Inorganic fillers (Dispersed Phase):
chunks.text:
2. Inorganic fillers (Dispersed Phase):
Fillers size:
1. Macro-filled (conventional).
2. Micro-filled.
3. Micro-hybrid.
4. Nano-hybrid.
5. Nano-filled.
Fillers size:
 Composites with large filler size produce rough surface.
 Decreasing the filler size produce smoother surface after
polishing but the finer particles have higher surface area.
 This high surface area leads to lower filler addidtion to
matrix.

chunks.heading: 2. Inorganic fillers (Dispersed Phase):

Fillers Size:
↑ Filler size → ↑ % of Fillers, ↓ Aesthetics & ↑ mechanical
properties.
↑ matrix → ↑ polymerization shrinkage, ↑ coefficient of thermal
expansion, ↑ water sorption
