chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 3- Coupling agents:
chunks.text:
3- Coupling agents:
The usually used coupling agent is vinyl silane
It is molecule with two functional groups:
 Organic group bonds with matrix

 Inorganic group bonds with fillers

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 3- Coupling agents:
chunks.text:
3- Coupling agents:
Functions:
Binds the organic matrix with the inorganic fillers in order
to:
1. Transfer the stresses from the weak matrix to the
stronger filler improving the mechanical properties.
2. Prevent water penetration between matrix & fillers
increasing hydrolytic stability.
3. Reduce early loss of fillers during service.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 4. Initiator –Activator system
chunks.text:
4. Initiator –Activator system
Polymerization reaction of resin composite is activated by:
1. Chemical activation.
2. Light activation.
3. Dual cure.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 4. Initiator –Activator system
chunks.text:
4. Initiator –Activator system
1. Chemical Cured Composite resin:
 It is supplied as 2 paste to be mixed:

a) One paste contains initiator (benzoyl peroxide).
b) The other contains activator (tertiary amine).

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 4. Initiator –Activator system
chunks.text:
4. Initiator –Activator system
2. Light Cured Composite resin:
 It is supplied as single paste that requires no mixing.

 Blue visible light (wavelength ≈470 nm) activates the
polymerization reaction.
 Initiator system is a mixture of diketone (as
camphorquinone ) and amine.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 4. Initiator –Activator system
chunks.text:
4. Initiator –Activator system
Advantages of Light Cured Composite over Chemical Cured
types
1. No human variations as there is no mixing
2. No air bubbles.
3. Command setting time.
4. More color stability.
5. Less polymerization shrinkage ( incrementally cured)

3. Dual Cured Composite resin:
 Contains initiator & accelerators that allow light
activation followed by self curing.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 5. Polymerization Inhibitors
chunks.text:
5. Polymerization Inhibitors

 Inhibitors such as hydroquinone are added to the
monomers to inhibit the premature polymerization
reaction of the monomers during storage or accidental
exposure to light.

 Eugenol inhibits polymerization of resin . So bases
containing eugenol should not be used as base under
composite.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 6. Ultraviolet Stabilizers
chunks.text:
6. Ultraviolet Stabilizers

 Added to prevent discoloration (Yellowish) with time of
resin composite restorations as they adsorb ultraviolet
radiation.

7. Pigments
 Inorganic pigments are added to give the different shades
of resin composite.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Properties of Resin Composite
chunks.text:
Properties of Resin Composite
1. Polymerization shrinkage.
2. Bonding to tooth structure.
3. Thermal properties.
4. Mechanical properties.
5. Aesthetics and optical properties.
6. Solubility.
7. Water sorption.
8. Biological properties.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 1. Polymerization shrinkage
chunks.text:
1. Polymerization shrinkage

 The matrix of resin composite undergo shrinkage during
its polymerization which causes stresses inside the
restoration.
 The polymerization increased as the amount of matrix
increased.
 So microfine shrink more than hybrid and nano-filled
types.
 If the polymerization stresses are higher than bond
strength :
Bond failure → Gap formation → Microleakage → Recurrent
caries and hypersensitivity

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 1. Polymerization shrinkage
chunks.text: 1. Polymerization shrinkage

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 1. Polymerization shrinkage
chunks.text:
1. Polymerization shrinkage
Methods of decreasing polymerization shrinkage:
1. Incremental addition of light cured resin composite and
polymerization of each increment independently.
2. Strong bond with tooth structure.
3. Indirect composite restoration:
The restoration is cured outside the mouth then cemented
by resin cement to tooth structure.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 2-Bonding to tooth structure
chunks.text:
2-Bonding to tooth structure
 Resin composite bonds micro mechanically with tooth
structure by acid etching technique.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 3-Thermal properties
chunks.text:
3-Thermal properties
a) Coefficient of thermal expansion and contraction:
 The higher the amount of matrix , the higher the coefficient
of thermal expansion (the greater the change in dimensions
due to changes in oral temperatures) causing more marginal
leakage).
 Therefore, micro-filled resin composite has higher coefficient
than hybrid & nano-filled types.

b)Thermal conductivity:
 Thermal conductivity of composites closely matches those of
enamel & dentin.
 Therefore they provide good thermal insulation for dental
pulp.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 4- Mechanical properties
chunks.text:
4- Mechanical properties
 Increasing the fillers amount improves the mechanical
properties.
 Micro-filled composite has inferior mechanical properties
compared with hybrid and nano filled types.

5- Aesthetics and optical properties
 Resin composite is a translucent material that can match
tooth color.
 It is supplied in different shades for more simulation of
natural teeth.
 Nano-filled composite has high translucency as the fillers
size is smaller than light wavelength.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: 6- Solubility
chunks.text:
6- Solubility
 It has lower solubility.

 The solubility resulting from release of residual monomers.

7- Water Sorption
 Resin matrix is responsible for water sorption .

 Micro-filled composite showed more water sorption than hybrid
and nano-filled types.

8.Biological Properties
 Residual monomers & uncured deep layers may cause chemical
irritation of the dental pulp.
 Rough surface of restoration may lead to plaque accumulation.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Low shrinkage Resin composite
chunks.text:
Low shrinkage Resin composite
1. Ormocer (Organically Modified Ceramics):
 The matrix is formed of organic- inorganic copolymer

 This copolymer is consisting of a siloxane backbone and an
organic methacrylate side chains connected to the
siloxane backbone.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Low shrinkage Resin composite
chunks.text:
Low shrinkage Resin composite
1. Ormocer (Organically Modified Ceramics):
 During curing, the organic methacrylate side chains
undergo free radical addition polymerization.
 The siloxane molecule is longer than Bis-GMA molecule
which is responsible for the lower polymerization
shrinkage of ormocer.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Low shrinkage Resin composite
chunks.text:
Low shrinkage Resin composite
1. Ormocer (Organically Modified Ceramics):
 Advantages of Ormocer:

1. Low polymerization shrinkage.
2. Highly biocompatible.
3. Good esthetics.
4. More depth of polymerization.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Low shrinkage Resin composite
chunks.text:
Low shrinkage Resin composite
2.Silorane:
 The matrix is siloxane and oxyrane.

 The terminal group is ring instead of double bond.

 It is polymerized by ring opening polymerization reaction.

 Polymerization shrinkage less than 1%.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Low shrinkage Resin composite
chunks.text:
Low shrinkage Resin composite
2.Silorane:

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Bulk –fill Composites
chunks.text:
Bulk –fill Composites

 This is a special type of composite that is able to build –up the
restorations in bulky layers up to 4 mm in thickness.
 The effective depth of curing and polymerization stresses are the main
problems facing this type.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Packable Resin Composite
chunks.text:
Packable Resin Composite
 It is high viscosity resin composite.

 Used for posterior restorations and core build up.

Advantages:
1. Packing against matrix allowing good proximal contact
formation.
2. Non-sticky.
Disadvantages:
1. Poor adaptation to the cavity wall due to high viscosity.
2. Opaquer than hybrid resin composite with comparable
mechanical properties.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Flowable Resin Composite
chunks.text:
Flowable Resin Composite
 It is low viscosity composite.

 It is dispensed into cavity by syringe with needle tip.

 Used as a liner or for cervical lesion restorations.

 Low viscosity is achieved by decreasing filler content.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Flowable Resin Composite
chunks.text:
Flowable Resin Composite
 Advantages:

1. Better adaptation to the cavity wall due to lower
viscosity.
2. Lower polymerization stresses due to lower elastic
modulus (causes stress relaxation).
 Disadvantages:

1. Lower mechanical properties.
2. High polymerization shrinkage.

chunks.title: Resin Composite Restorative Materials
chunks.heading: Classification or Resin Composite
chunks.text:
Classification or Resin Composite
1.According to particle size & shape:
a) Fine Composite
b) Micro-fine Composite
c) Hybrid Composite 3. According to viscosity:
d) Nano-hybrid Composite a) Conventional composite
e) Nano-filled Composite b) Packable Composite
c) Flowable composite
2.According to method of curing:
a) Chemically cured composite
b) Light cured composite
c) Dual cured composite

chunks.heading: Dental Cements
chunks.text:
Dental Cements
Marwa Bahaa
Lecturer of dental biomaterials

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Application of dental cements
chunks.text:
Application of dental cements
1. Cavity lining and base under restorations.
2. Luting applications i.e. cementation of crowns,
bridges, inlays, onlays and orthodontic brackets.
“temporary or permanent”.
3. Some cements are specifically formulated to be
used as temporary or permanent filling materials.
4. Certain other cements for specialized purposes in
the endodontic, periodontic and surgical fields of
dentistry.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Application of dental cements
chunks.text: Application of dental cements

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
chunks.text:
Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
1. Biological properties:
a) Non-toxic and non-irritant to the pulp and other oral
tissues.
b) It should be obtundent (alleviate pulpal irritation &pain),
palliative, and sedative to oral tissues.
c) It should be bacteriostatic.
d) It should provide thermal insulation.
e) It should provide chemical insulation.
f) It should provide electrical insulation.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
chunks.text:
Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
2. Rheological properties:
a) The luting cement should have thin film
thickness.
b) The cement should have a good working time
and short setting time.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
chunks.text:
Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
2. Rheological properties:
The cement film thickness depends on:
1. The powder particle size: finer powder particle size →
a lower film thickness.
2. The viscosity of the mix: depends on the P/L ratio.
Using more liquid for mixing results in a less viscous
(more flowable) cement mix → easily flushed into a low
film thickness during seating of the restoration.
3. The amount of pressure applied on the restoration
during cementation: Using more pressure allows better
seating with less film thickness.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
chunks.text:
Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
3. Solubility:
 The cement should be insoluble in oral fluids to prevent
leakage, loosening of the restoration and recurrent caries.

4. Mechanical properties:
 Mechanical requirements vary according to uses of dental
cements.
e.g. if used as a liner should develop strength rapidly Why??
to enable filling material to be packed over it.
 The strength of the cement depends on its composition
and W/P %.
 Base under amalgam should have sufficient strength why??
To withstand condensation force of amalgam.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
chunks.text:
Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
5. Bonding:
 The cement should bond to tooth structure and to
restorations by either:
a) Mechanical interlocking: the freshly mixed cement flows
into the microscopic irregularities on the tooth and
restoration surface then hardens.
b) Chemical bonding: the freshly mixed cement forms a
chemical bond with the tooth and the restoration surface.
 Chemical adhesion is considered as gold standard for bonding.

 Cements with chemical bonding are described as “adhesive”.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
chunks.text:
Ideal Requirements of dental Cements
5. Optical properties:
The optical requirements also depend on the application of
the dental cement:
1. If used for cementing opaque restoration e.g. all metallic
crown: either opaque or translucent cement.
2. If used for cementing translucent restoration: only
translucent cement can be used.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
 It is one of the earliest cements used in dentistry.

Mode of supply:
A. Powder and liquid: for cementation.
B. Ready-made single paste: as temporary filling.
C. Two paste: for temporary cementation.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Composition of Type I :
A. Powder:
Zinc oxide + 8 % zinc as accelerator+ Rosin to reduce
brittleness and increase working time and strength.
B. Liquid:
Eugenol + acetic acid as accelerator

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Setting reaction:
ZnO + H₂O → Zn(OH)₂

Zn(OH)₂+ eugenol → Zn eugenolate + H₂O

It is called chelation reaction.
Microstructure:
The set material consists of unreacted zinc
oxide and free eugenol in a zinc
eugenolate matrix.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Setting reaction:
 Water is essential for the setting reaction to occurs as ZnO
cannot react with eugenol. Only zinc hydroxide can react
with eugenol.
 Humidity and heat accelerate the reaction.

 Ready –made single paste contains no water and start to
set after contact with moisture inside patient mouth.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Manipulation:
Powder and liquid:
 Mixing using stainless-steel spatula over glass slab or oil
resistant pad.
 The P/L ratio depends on the required viscosity and use.

 Powder is added incrementally to the liquid.

Two pastes:
 Dispense equal lengths and mix until obtain homogenous
color.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Properties:
1. Biological properties:
 The set cement is neutral (pH=7).

 The eugenol has sedative , palliative and obtundent effect
on the pulp.
 Eugenol has a bacteriostatic action.

 Avoid high conc. Of eugenol to avoid inflammation.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement

2. Consistency & film thickness:
 Film thickness= 40 microns which is high compared to the

3. Solubility:

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:

5. Bonding:

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Limitations:
Zinc oxide eugenol cement:
1-Shouldn’t be used as base under composite resin why???
2-Not as temporary filling for teeth that will be restored
with composite resin. Why???
3- Not as temporary cement for crown on teeth to be
restored using composite resin cement.
Why??? Because : ZnO is opaque
Eugenol inhibit polymerization reaction.

chunks.title: Dental Cements — Part 1
chunks.heading: Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
chunks.text:
Zinc Oxide and Eugenol Cement
Limitations:
 The unmodified form has lower mechanical properties and
high solubility. Therefore, it cannot be used base under
amalgam restoration why???.

 Eugenol containing cement is contra-indicated to be used
for temporary cementation for teeth to be restored with
all ceramic restoration , why?????
As all ceramic restoration is cemented finally by resin
cement, any remnants from eugenol will inhibit the
polymerization reaction of final resin cement .

hydrated zinc phosphate matrix.

 The reaction is rapid and exothermic

Classification
 The most practical and widely used classification of GICs
is based on their clinical application.
 According to this classification, there are three main
types of GICs:
Type I: GICs used for luting applications.
Type II: GICs used as restorative materials.
Type III: GICs used as liners or bases.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Setting reaction
Acid-base reaction .
 Once the powder and liquid are mixed together, the
reaction goes through the following three stages:
1.Dissolution
2.Migration
3.Reaction And Precipitation

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Setting reaction:
1.Dissolution:
 Dissolution of the surface of glass by acid.

 H+ attacks the powder particles and dissolve the outer
layer (20% to 30 % of the particles are dissolved).
 Na+, Ca++ ,Al+++ and F- ions are released while the SiO₂
remains on the outer layer of the particles.
 Ca++and Al+++ are responsible for cross linking the acid
chains while Na+ and F- are released from the cement as
NaF

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Setting reaction
2. Migration:
 Migration of the released surface ions (Ca++ ,Al+++ and F-
)into the liquid.
 The divalent calcium ions migrate first followed by
trivalent Al ions.
 The sodium ions form silica gel on the surface of the glass
particles.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Setting reaction:
3. Reaction and precipitation:
Ca++
 The migrating Ca ++ ions react first with the carboxylic
groups of the acid to form a cross-linked polycarboxylic
salt gel.
 Each Ca ++ ion is divalent and can only cross-link two
polycarboxylic chains.
 This results in a relatively weak cross-linked gel.

 This early Ca-mediated cross linking only leads to an
“initial set” of the glass ionomer.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Setting reaction:
3. Reaction and precipitation:
Al+++ :
 followed by the reaction of the slowly migrating trivalent
Al +++ ions.
 Being trivalent, each Al +++ ion can cross-link three
polycarboxylic chains more effective cross linking
and formation of a stronger gel.
 This last reaction takes longer time (up to 24 hours) and
results in the “final set” of the cement

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Setting reaction:
3. Reaction and precipitation:
 The water is bonded to silica gel (SiO₂) at the outer layer
of the particles.
 This reaction takes long time (up to 24 h).

 Therefore ,the cement should be protected against
premature exposure to saliva why?? as it affects the
setting and the surface hardness of the cement.

 It serves initially as a reaction medium and is loosely

 It slowly hydrates the cross-linked matrix and becomes
tightly bound, thereby,
 Increasing the material strength by producing a stable gel
structure.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Glass Ionomer Cement
chunks.text:
Glass Ionomer Cement
Modifications

Modification to glass ionomer cement were invented to
overcome its limitations such as :

1. Initial low strength.
2. Initial water sensitivity.
3. Long setting time.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: 1.Metal modified Glass Ionomer
chunks.text:
1.Metal modified Glass Ionomer
1. Metal-modified glass ionomer (Cermet):
 This modification is mainly related to the powder.

 Fine particles of precious metals (such as silver, gold or
palladium) are sintered with the glass ionomer powder
particles.
 Silver is the most commonly used metal.
 The liquid has the same composition as the liquid used
for the conventional GIC.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: 1.Metal modified Glass Ionomer
chunks.text:
1.Metal modified Glass Ionomer
1. Metal-modified glass ionomer (Cermet):
Advantages (Compared to conventional GIC):
1. Higher abrasion resistance (resists wear).
2. Higher flexure strength .
3. Higher fracture toughness (resists crack propagation).
Drawbacks (Compared to conventional GIC):
1. More opaque because of their metal content.
2. Release less fluoride.
Uses: Cermets can be used as:
1. Core build up material.
2. Filling material for class I and II cavities in deciduous
teeth.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: 2. Resin modified Glass Ionomer (RMGIC)
chunks.text:
2. Resin modified Glass Ionomer (RMGIC)
 Moisture sensitivity and a low early strength of conventional glass
ionomer cements are the result of the slow nature of the acid-
base setting reaction.
To overcome this
 Polymerizable functional groups were incorporated into the
cement to impart more rapid curing when activated by light or
chemicals. Thus, these materials set by a polymerization
reaction & the acid-base reaction that continues long after
polymerization.

Resin Cements
1. Conventional resin composite cement:
 They are composed of resinous matrix, fillers, initiator

restoration and tooth structure. Therefore, acid etching
and bonding agents are required for cementing the
restorations.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer

chunks.text:
Resin Cements

Conventional resin composite cements may be further
classified into three types according to the curing
mechanism:

A. Self cured
B. Light cured
C. Dual cured

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Resin Cements
chunks.text:
Resin Cements
I-Self-cured resin composite cements:
 powder/liquid or two paste systems.

 Diacrylate oligomer diluted with lower molecular weight
dimethacrylate monomer is a major component .
 The other major component is silanated silica or glass
filler.
 The reaction is initiated by peroxide-amine initiator
accelerator system.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Resin Cements
chunks.text:
Resin Cements
II- Light-cured resin composite cements:
 A paste which requires no mixing.

 One major component of the cement is Bis-GMA or
urethane dimethacrylate diluted with lower molecular
weight dimethacrylate monomer.
 The other major component is fumed silica or glass fillers
(20%-75% by weight) or both.
 A camphorquinone-amine photo-initiator system is
included.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Resin Cements
chunks.text:
Resin Cements
III- Dual-cure resin composite cements:
 Their composition is similar to the light-cured type .

 They polymerize by the two mechanisms of setting, the
light and the chemical curing at the same time.
 They are supplied as base-catalyst paste and must be
mixed before use.
 After mixing, a self-cure polymerization reaction takes
place slowly and provides extended working time until the
cement is exposed to light , then the cement sets rapidly
by a photopolymerization reaction.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Resin Cements
chunks.text:
Resin Cements
2- Self Adhesive resin cements:
 These are resin cements formulated with an adhesion promoter:

 For example adhesion promoter called (4 META).

 Another available adhesive resin cements systems achieves chemical
bonding to the tooth structure via phosphonate groups.
 The phosphate end of the phosphonate reacts with the calcium of the
tooth or with the metal oxide layer on the restoration surface.
 The phosphonate is very sensitive to oxygen which inhibits its
polymerization, so a gel called “oxyguard” is provided to coat the
margins of the restoration until the setting of the cement is
completed.

chunks.title: Dental Cements Part 2 — Glass Ionomer
chunks.heading: Resin Cements
chunks.text:
Resin Cements
2- Self Adhesive resin cements:
 Self-adhesive resin cement is a class of resin-based cements that
incorporates the etching, priming, and bonding chemistry in a single
material.
 No need for separate etching and bonding steps, The self-adhesive
resin cements were designed specifically to interact with the dentin
substrate with minimal additional surface preparation.
 However, the bond to enamel is not as strong as with the use of
phosphoric acid etchants. If many enamel margins are present, it is
often recommended to etch with phosphoric acid even while using
these cements.
 Self adhesive resin cements show good bond strength values to metal
alloys and high-strength ceramics.

Copolymers
- Copolymers are fabricated to modify the physical and chemical properties
of the polymer network.
- For example, in denture bases, copolymerization of the monomers of methyl

methacrylate + butyl methacrylate results in a copolymer that is more
fracture resistant.

- Addition of comonomers such as octyl methacrylate makes the copolymer soft and
flexible, and these copolymers are used for denture soft liners.

- Addition of hydroxyethyl methacrylate increases the wettability of the polymer by
water and improves complete denture retention in a patient with xerostomia (dry
mouth).

chunks.heading: Occupational safety:
chunks.text:
Occupational safety:
• The volatile nature of monomers and the dusty nature of the
fine PMMA particles may result in professional hazards to the
dental staff .

• -To reduce the concentration of monomer vapors and
exposure in dental clinics and laboratories, appropriate safety
measures are essential :- such as the use of personal
protection (mask, gloves, googles, face shield) and airtight
containers, , good ventilation, and quick disposal of any spills .
•
• -In addition, dental staff should be educated about the toxic
and volatile nature of monomer solution (no exposure to
flames) and immediate washing of the skin if exposed to the
monomer solution + medical advice in case of direct exposure

• -Chronic inhalation of methyl methacrylate should be
avoided because of potential toxicity to the liver

chunks.heading: Soft liners
chunks.text:
Soft liners
Denture soft liners are materials that coat the tissue-bearing surface of a
complete or partial denture.

these materials are soft or rubbery and are less likely to traumatize the oral
soft tissues.

Soft liners are used for patients with severe undercuts of the edentulous
ridges or for those patients whose ridges are continually sore.

They also are useful as a tissue treatment after oral surgery and in obturators
for congenital or acquired defects of the palate, such as cleft palate or post
surgery for oral-facial cancer.

chunks.title: Polymer Denture Base Materials & Soft Liners
chunks.heading: I- LONG TERM SOFT LINERS:
chunks.text:
I- LONG TERM SOFT LINERS:
- Long-term materials are commonly methacrylate- or silicone-based polymers.

- A-Methacrylate-based materials: often consist of poly(methyl/ethyl methacrylate)
copolymers with plasticizers.
- Plasticizers are not generally chemically bonded to the polymer network

- Methacrylate-based liners are cured either by heat or chemically at room temperature, depending
on their formulation.

- Heat-cured formulations are processed in a laboratory, whereas chemical-cure materials may be
processed either in the laboratory or at chairside.

The hardness of the long-term acrylic materials increases slowly as the plasticizer is
leached out by exposure to oral fluids.

chunks.title: Polymer Denture Base Materials & Soft Liners
chunks.heading: B-Silicone-based polymers :
chunks.text:
B-Silicone-based polymers :
They are also are used as long-term soft liners.

Silicone soft liners are either heat cured or chemical
cured, but they are processed in a laboratory
regardless of the initiation mechanism.

Unlike methacrylate-based liners, silicone
liners do not harden as time passes because
they contain no plasticizer.

Clinically, silicone liners may support the
growth of Candida albicans (yeast)

chunks.title: Polymer Denture Base Materials & Soft Liners
chunks.heading: II- SHORT TERM SOFT LINERS:
chunks.text:
II- SHORT TERM SOFT LINERS:
Short-term materials are used in clinical situations in which the edentulous
tissues are inflamed or swollen

Short-term lining materials consist of a polyethylene methacrylate
powder and liquid plasticizers. When
these materials are mixed, there is no polymerization
reaction

Short-term materials, also known as “treatment” materials, are
always applied at chairside, and the liner is replaced frequently (every
3 days or sooner)

They become harder as the oral fluids leach out the plasticizers.

chunks.title: Polymer Denture Base Materials & Soft Liners
chunks.heading: Denture care
chunks.text:
Denture care
Complete or partial dentures should be removed each night
and cleaned to ensure the health of the supporting oral
tissues.

Q:When removed from the mouth, dentures must remain wet and are best stored in
water. Why??
Answer: 1-Because acrylic polymers have high water sorption, desiccation results in a
significant loss of water and shrinkage of the polymer.

2-If cycles of hydration and desiccation continue, the denture will
gradually distort and crazing would appear.

chunks.title: Odontogenesis — Development & Growth of Teeth
chunks.heading: A tooth germ consists of 3 parts:
chunks.text:
A tooth germ consists of 3 parts:
1. Enamel organ; derived from the oral ectoderm &
produces the enamel.
2. Dental papilla, derived from the ectomesenchyme &
produces dentin & pulp.
3. Dental sac (tooth follicle); derived from
ectomesenchyme & produces cementum, PDL & alveolar
bone.

Dental organ, dental papilla and dental
follicle together constitutes the tooth germ.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: Bell stage
chunks.text:
Bell stage
Constitutes 2 phases :
1) Early bell stage: Before the start of
formation of mineralized tissues.
2) Late (Advanced) bell stage: Starts
once the 1st layer of dentin is laid down.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: Early bell stage
chunks.text:
Early bell stage
Histological feature of Early bell stage:
D. Papilla continues to increase in size &
D. organ continues to encircle it.
D. organ assumes a bell shape
deciding the type of the future tooth.
This bell shape resulted from
differential growth
between inner & outer D. epithelia,
In which the outer D. epithelium
proliferation rate is more than
that of inner D. epithelium.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: Dental Organ:
chunks.text:
Dental Organ:
Dental organ shows more histodifferentiation &
morpho-differentiation than in cap stage.
A) Outer D. epithelium:
Low cuboidal cells arranged on the convex side of the D. organ.
-Functions: Regulate transport & exchange of substances between D. organ &
D. Sac.

B) Stellate reticulum:
Several layers of expanded star shaped cells with intercellular spaces filled with
mucopolysaccharides between inner & outer D. epithelia. They expand
more than in cap stage by increasing the intercellular fluid.

Functions:
1) Mechanical: Absorbs the pressure generated by the expanding surrounding
mesoderm to protect the sensitive ameloblasts (acts as cushion).
2) Nutritive: Act as store house for nutrition (mainly minerals) needed for enamel-
forming cells (Ameloblast).
3) Keeps room for the developing enamel

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: C) Stratum intermedium:
chunks.text:
C) Stratum intermedium:
2-3 layers of flat cells differentiated between inner D.
epithelium & stellate reticulum characterized by high activity of
alkaline phosphatase enzyme
Functions:
1) Controls of diffusion of materials to ameloblast.
2) Provides the enamel organ with enzymes needed for formation
& mineralization of enamel especially alkaline phosphatase
enzyme.

D) Inner dental epithelium:
Tall columnar epithelial cells with apical nucleus.
Cells located at the inner concavity of D. organ and characterized
by high Glycogen content.
* Most of elongation is toward D. papilla resulting in
disappearance of cell free zone.

chunks.heading: Early Bell Stage
chunks.text:
Early Bell Stage

chunks.heading: * Inner D. epithelium has an organizing effect on the
chunks.text:
* Inner D. epithelium has an organizing effect on the
UMCs to differentiate into odontoblast. This process is called
Induction.
-Functions:
1) Regulate the transport of substances from D. papilla
to D. organ (before hard dental tissue formation).
2) Determines the morphology of the future dentino-
enamel junction.
3) Induce UMCs of D.P. to differentiate into
odontoblasts.
4) Join with outer dental epith. to form the cervical loop
(area of active cell proliferation which will form epithelial
diaphragm & epithelial root sheath of Hertwig).

chunks.heading: II) Dental papilla shows :
chunks.text:
II) Dental papilla shows :
There is an increase in size of the dental papilla
enclosed by invaginated portion of inner D. epithelium.
Dental papilla is formed of:
A) Cells: Includes UMCs & odontoblasts on periphery
(when inner D. epithelium induces the peripheral UMCs)
B) Intercellular (extracellular) substance:
1) Ground substance.
2) few scattered collagen fibrils.
C) increase in number of capillary loops.

chunks.heading: At the end of early bell stage:
chunks.text:
At the end of early bell stage:
Basement membrane separating inner D.
epith & odontoblast is thickened & called
Membrana preformativa
-Functions of D.papilla:
1) Nutrition for D. organ.
2) UMCs differentiated into odontoblasts which
will form dentin.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: III) Dental sac (Dental follicle) shows:
chunks.text:
III) Dental sac (Dental follicle) shows:
It Surround D. org & D. papilla.
It is composed of an inner layer is relatively more
cellular & lies close to outer D. epithelium & D. papilla. And
an outer layer is less cellular & lies against walls of bony crypt.
Also, it shows aground substance full of collagen
fibrils between fibroblast (fibroblasts in dental follicle) which
are generally oriented in a pattern around D. organ & D.
papilla.
-Functions:
Provides sufficient support and protection to
prevent distortion of outer D. epithelium.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: Late bell stage
chunks.text:
Late bell stage
Histological feature of advanced (late) Bell stage:
1) Marked by beginning of dentin formation &
mineralization.
2) The boundary between inner D. epithelium &
odontoblasts outlines the future DEJ (Dentino-
enamel junction).
3) Later, the cervical loop gives rise to epithelium
Diaphragm [E.D.] which will give rise to epithelial
root sheath of Hertwig [ERSH] which is important
for root formation.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: I) Dental organ:
chunks.text:
I) Dental organ:
A) Outer D. epithelium: Cells get flattened to be
low cuboidal or flat on the outer side of D. organ.
This layer shows infoldings with
many blood capillaries between these
folds.
Functions:
1. Regulate transport & exchange of substances
between D. organ & D. Sac.
2. it becomes included as a part of reduced dental
epithelium (or reduced enamel epithelium).
The reduced dental epithelium contains all cells of
dental organ

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: B) Inner D. epithelium: Tall columnar cells
chunks.text:
B) Inner D. epithelium: Tall columnar cells
on the inner side of D. organ & facing the formed
Dentin.
Differentiate to become active secretory
cells called ameloblasts which produce
Enamel matrix that eventually mineralize to
enamel.
Reciprocal induction:
Enamel formation cannot begin till some
dentin is formed (by odontoblasts) and
Odontoblasts differentiate under organizing
influence stemming from inner D. epithelium.

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: Functions:
chunks.text:
Functions:
1) At the end of Enamel formation, it becomes
included as a part of RDE.
2) Differentiate to Ameloblast that will
form enamel matrix that eventually mineralize
to Enamel.
3)Ameloblast secretes an organic layer on
the fully matured Enamel
called primary enamel cuticle
(Nasmyth membrane).

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: C) Stellate Reticulum:
chunks.text:
C) Stellate Reticulum:
Star shaped cells between stratum intermedium
& outer D. epith.
As 1st Dentin is laid down, the stellate reticulum
layer is markedly reduced in thickness
due to loss of intercellular fluid.
- Functions:1) Mechanical: Absorbs the pressure
generated by the expanding surrounding mesoderm to
protect the sensitive ameloblasts (acts as cushion).
2) Nutritive: Act as store house for nutrition
(mainly minerals) needed for enamel-forming cells
(Ameloblast).
3) Keeps room for the developing enamel

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: D) Stratum Intermedium:
chunks.text:
D) Stratum Intermedium:
2-3 Rows of flat cells between inner D.
epithelium & stellate reticulum.
Provides Alkaline phosphatase enzyme
(important for enamel mineralization).
Functions:
1) Controls of diffusion of materials to ameloblast.
2) Provides the enamel organ with enzymes needed for
formation & mineralization of enamel especially alkaline
phosphatase enzyme.
(Stratum intermedium & Ameloblast are
considered the functional unit for production
of enamel)

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: II) Dental papilla:
chunks.text:
II) Dental papilla:
Dental Papilla is termed as "dental pulp" when
dentin begins to be formed.
dental pulp is composed of:
A) Cells → UMCs & odontoblasts.
B) Intercellular substance ground substance & fibrils
C) Blood capillaries

chunks.title: The Cap Stage of Tooth Development
chunks.heading: III) Dental Sac:
chunks.text:
III) Dental Sac:
increased condensation of fibers and cells surrounding D. org &
D. papilla.
Mesenchyme of D. sac invades the D. lamina joining the
tooth germ to oral epith. leading to Destruction of D.
Lamina loss of connection between the growing tooth
germ and oral epithelium.
Remnants of dental lamina may persist in gingiva & jaw
and called epithelial rest of Serre's. (Serre's pearls).
Serre's pearls normally degenerate Or may form small cyst over
the developing tooth that delays the eruption.
- Functions:
Provides sufficient support and protection to prevent
distortion of outer D. epithelium.

resorbed.

chunks.title: Root Formation & Hertwig's Epithelial Root Sheath
chunks.heading: Possible causes are: Accessory Root Canal
chunks.text:
Possible causes are: Accessory Root Canal
1) Defective formation of epithelial root sheath of Hertwig (ERSH).
2) Premature degeneration of ERSH before differentiation of odontoblasts
which leads to defect in the dentinal wall of pulp chamber or root canal.
3) Displaced blood vessel.
4) Failure in fusion of tongue like projections of epithelial diaphragm.

However, the presence of few cells stratum intermedium & stellate
reticulum is essential for formation of E. pearl.

E. rods run from DEJ straight then follows a wavy

chunks.heading: Modulation
chunks.text:
Modulation
The cyclic creation, loss & recreation of a highly invaginated
ruffle-ended apical surface. The cell alternate between having a
ruffled border (brush border) or smooth border.

• The ruffle- ended ameloblasts have:
• Leaky proximal junctions & tight distal junctions.
• Ca binding proteins & membrane Ca ATPase
(promote Ca pumping).
• Promote pumping of Ca ions into the maturing enamel.

chunks.heading: Modulation
chunks.text:
Modulation
•Smooth-ended ameloblasts:
leaky distal junctions,
•Have
tight proximal ones.

chunks.text:
6-Protective & Desmolytic stage
• When the E. has completely developed & fully calcified ,The
ameloblasts with the other cells of the E. organ forming the reduced
enamel epithelium.(REE)

• REE protects the newly formed enamel surface till
time of eruption & It helps in tooth eruption.

• Enamel may be resorbed or cementum deposited on
enamel surface.

chunks.title: Life History of Ameloblasts
chunks.heading: Protective stage
chunks.text:
Protective stage
• Layers of epithelial dental organs form a
stratified epithelial covering of the enamel
Known Reduced Enamel Epithelium. Reduced enamel epithelium

• This layer protects enamel before eruption from

being resorbed or attacked by cells of

the dental sac which may form

cementum on it.

chunks.title: Life History of Ameloblasts
chunks.heading: Desmolytic stage
chunks.text:
Desmolytic stage
The reduced enamel epithelium secrete
desmolytic enzymes that induce
atrophy and destruction of the
connective tissue separating it from the
oral epithelium, so
fusion of the two epithelia can occur to
facilitate tooth eruption.

Abfraction
Recently, it has been proposed that the predominant causative
factor of some of the cervical, wedge-shaped defects is a strong
(heavy) eccentric occlusal force resulting in microfracture
occure at the cervical area of the tooth.
This defects is termed
as idiopathic erosion

chunks.heading: 2-Permeability
chunks.text:
2-Permeability
Enamel is semi-permeable, allowing ionic exchange which leads
to its surface modification.
Enamel crystals may acquire more ions reducing the size of the pores
between them. This leads to decreased permeability.
The permeability decreases or even disappears from the outer surface,
while that from the dentinal surface may remain.

Recently Old enamel
Erupted teeth

chunks.heading: 3- Color changes of the tooth
chunks.text:
3- Color changes of the tooth
Normally with age it become more yellowish as
minerals more perciptated & also may it
associated with internal calcification.
It may also be due to attrition exposing the yellow
color of dentin(which become thicker & sclerotic) through
the thinning layer of enamel with reducing its
translucency.
Teeth color gradually darken with age due to the
addition of organic material to enamel from the
environment (tobacco, coffee & tea) Due to
permeability.

chunks.title: Amelogenesis — Matrix Formation & Mineralization
chunks.heading: 4- Modification in the surface layer
chunks.text:
4- Modification in the surface layer
After tooth eruption, enamel undergo modification in the surface layer
(ionic exchange) between enamel & saliva (alteration in the chemical
composition of enamel). This may lead to localized increase of certain
elements (e.g. fluorine & nitrogen) in the superficial enamel layer by age.
This exchange increases the inorganic content to be 98% called (2ry maturation)
A decrease of the water content of enamel by age was also suggested.
These alternations may lead to
reduction in the enamel porosity &
caries incidence.
Which means that enamel near the surface
become decay resistant.

Then increase the porosity of exposed surfaces by selective dissolution of

chunks.text:
The dentinal tubules are:
 Closely backed together at the pulpal surface than the outer surface with a ratio per unit
area 4:1.
 The diameter of dentinal tubules is narrower at the outer surface (1 micron) than the
pulpal surface (2-3 micron).
 The course of dentinal tubules from the pulp surface to the outer surface takes an S
shape which is called primary curvature (the first convexity facing root ward).
 In the root portion and under the tip of the cusp or incisal edge, the dentinal tubules
take a straight course.
 Each dentinal tubule shows small secondary curvature along its course which resulted
from the spiral track taken by the odontoblastic process during its course from the outer
surface of dentine to the pulp surface.

chunks.heading: Periodontoblastic space.
chunks.text:
Periodontoblastic space.
 It is the space between the odontoblastic

 The odontoblastic process and
periodontoblastic space are the soft

chunks.title: Dentin
chunks.heading: Inter–tubular dentine
chunks.text:
Inter–tubular dentine

 It forms the main body of dentine and is located between the
dentinal tubules.
 Represent the primary secretory product of odontoblasts.
 It consists oftightly interwoven network of type I collagen
fibers in amorphous ground substance in which apatite crystal
are deposited.
 In the first formed layer of dentine (mantle dentine) the collagen
fibers are arranged at right angle with the dentine surface.
 In the remaining part of dentine (circumpulpal dentine) the fibrils
are closely packed together in bundles which run parallel to the
dentine surface and have right or oblique angle to the dentinal
tubules.
 The crystals of dentine are formed in between the fibrils and
around them where their long axis is parallel to the fibrils
direction.

chunks.title: Dentin
chunks.heading: Peritubular dentine
chunks.text:
Peritubular dentine
 Highly calcified dentine.
 It is about 40% more mineralized than
intertubular dentine.
 It is deposited on the internal walls of the
dentinal tubules .
 In T S ground section through the dentinal
tubules shows that the peritubular dentine Is
seen as translucent rings.
 In decalcified section the odontoblastic process
will appear shrunken with ring shaped space
around it(because the highly calcified
peritubular dentine is totally dissolved.
 The organic fibrils of peritubular dentine are
continuous with those of inter-tubular dentine.

chunks.title: Dentin
chunks.heading: Pattern Of Mineralization
chunks.text:
Pattern Of Mineralization

 The calcification of the dentine matrix starts after formation of a fairly wide band of predentine (10-20μ)
and proceeds in a rate parallel to the matrix formation.
 Mineralization starts near to the D.E.J. as small islands which enlarge and fuse together to form a
continuous calcified layer of dentine.
 First the odontoblasts bud off small vesicles from their plasma membrane to the matrix. These matrix
vesicles are rich in calcium and phosphate ions and alkaline phosphatase enzyme.
 In these matrix vesicles the crystals are formed and then the vesicles will rupture and mineralize the
matrix.
 Mineralization has three patterns:
 1- Linear (occur in mantel dentine).
 2- Globular pattern (in circumpulpal dentine just below the mantel dentin) as globules which enlarge and
fuse together to form a calcified mass.
 3- Combination (in the rest of the circumpulpal dentine).

Dentine formation is a continuous process through out life but, it

dentine by odontoblast.

• Alterations by age & diseases which affect cellular function.
• Glycosaminoglycnas are bulky molecules & hydrophilic, they
form gels that fill most of the extracellular space, They contribute to
maintain the tissue fluid pressure of the pulp.

pulp has an abundant nerve supply which follows

Myelinated fibers

layer of nerves or plexus of Raschkow.
*More nerve endings are found in the pulp horns
than in other peripheral areas of the coronal or radicular pulp.

chunks.text:

Sensory response in the pulp cannot differentiate between
heat, touch, pressure or chemicals. This is because the pulp
organs lack those types of receptors.
Only type of the nerve receptors is FREE NERVE ENDING.

chunks.title: Dental Pulp
chunks.heading: 4- Protective
chunks.text:
4- Protective
Presence of rigid dentinal walls protect the pulp & presence of
junctional complexes between adjacent odontoblasts provide
strong points of cohesion between cells & prevent ingress of
bacteria & toxins to the pulp.
When such defenses fail to prevent access of the irritant to the
pulp & resolution of inflammation, defensive cells as (histiocytes,
T- lymphocytes & dendritic cells) are activated.

Sensory nerves in the tooth respond with pain to all
stimuli, Pain sensation is a useful alarm system of the pulp.

chunks.title: Dental Pulp
chunks.heading: 5- Defensive or reparative
chunks.text:
5- Defensive or reparative
Pulp responds to irritation by
producing reparative dentin and
mineralizing any affected dentinal
tubules.
●These reparative reactions are an
attempt to wall off the pulp from the
source of irritation.
Presence of macrophages,
lymphocytes and leucocytes aid in
the process of repair of the pulp.

Cementum could be classification
according to:
A. The presence or absence of cells within its matrix:
• Acellular cementum
• Cellular cementum
B. Time of formation
• Primary cementum
• Secondary cementum (after cementum formation reaching apex)
C. The origin of collagen fibers in the matrix
• Intrinsic fibers resulting from cementoblasts activity
• Extrinsic fibers resulting from the incorporation of periodontal ligament fibers

chunks.title: Cementum
chunks.heading: Primary acellular intrinsic fiber cementum
chunks.text:
Primary acellular intrinsic fiber cementum
• Forms 10% of acellular cementum

• Matrix: Is the result of cementoblast
(completely) activity and is elaborated before
formation of PDL so all collagen is intrinsic.

• Thickness and site: innermost 15-20μm of
cementum

• Function: Attachment of cementum & dentin
together

chunks.title: Cementum
chunks.heading: Primary acellular extrinsic fiber cementum
chunks.text:
Primary acellular extrinsic fiber cementum
• Forms 90% of acellular cementum

• Matrix: is formed after the PDL fibers connect to the fibrous
fring of primary acellular intrinsic fiber cementum.

• Thickness & site: extends form cervical line and covers almost
2/3s of the root forms the bulk of acellular cementum.

• Function: it is the principle tissue of attachment.

chunks.title: Cementum
chunks.heading: Secondary cellular intrinsic fiber cementum
chunks.text:
Secondary cellular intrinsic fiber cementum

• Matrix: Is a result of cementoblast activity and elaborated before PDL
formation the cells are incorporated into the matrix

• Thickness & site: confined to the apical 1/3 (may be absent in incisors and
canines)

• Function: involved in tooth attachment

• NB: increase rate of deposition → leads to trapped cells

chunks.title: Cementum
chunks.heading: Secondary cellular mixed fiber cementum
chunks.text:
Secondary cellular mixed fiber cementum
• Matrix: when PDL fibers are formed and organized it becomes incorporated
and cementum is deposited around ligament f. bundles which becomes
partially mineralized

• Thickness and site: Extremely variable thickness Forms the bulk of cellular
Cementum, Occupies apical & interradicular regions

• Function: adaptive tissue

• NB: cementoid layer is always present on the surface of cellular cementum

chunks.title: Cementum
chunks.heading: Mixed stratified cementum
chunks.text:
Mixed stratified cementum
• Matrix: consists of alternating layers of
acellular extrinsic & cellular intrinsic fiber
cementum

• Thickness & site: variable, found in apical
1/3 & furcation area

• Function: this alternating of cellular and
acellular occurs in response to adaptive
need.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: BONE
chunks.text:
BONE
Highly specialized Hard Connective tissue.
Consists of cells & Calcified intercellular substance (matrix &
fibers).
Locally, mechanical forces as tooth movement, growth
factors & cytokines also have regulatory functions.
Systemically, hormonal factors control the bone physiology.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Hormones that control the bone physiology.
chunks.text:
Hormones that control the bone physiology.
Parathyroid hormone stimulates
osteoclast resorption.
•Calcitonin and Estrogen inhibit bone
resorption.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Chemical composition
chunks.text:
Chemical composition
-67% inorganic
(small plates of hydroxyapatite crystals)

-33% organic
-28% type I collagen
-5% non-collagenous proteins

Bone sialoprotein , osteocalcin, osteonectin, osteopontin, proteoglycans & growth factors.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Functions of bone
chunks.text:
Functions of bone
1- Forms and Support the skeletal functions.

2- Bone protects the vital internal organs.
3- Provides attachment of the muscles & ligaments.
4- Bone stores minerals, especially calcium and
phosphorous, which are mobilized according to
the body needs. (containing 99% of body calcium).
5- Bone marrow manufactures the blood
elements. (Hemopoiesis).
6- Bone remodeling is responsible for the development,
growth, movements, fracture and repair.

chunks.text:
Bone Cells
2 cell lineages are present in bone:
1-osteogenic cells: form & maintain bone.
Osteoprogenitor cells (give osteoblasts).
Osteoblasts (secrete the extracellular matrix).
Osteocytes (mature cells enclosed by matrix).
2-Osteoclasts (bone resorbing cells)

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Osteoprogenitor cell (DiDi)
chunks.text:
Osteoprogenitor cell (DiDi)
Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells that have the
capacity to divide and differentiate to other bone cells

Location: Present in the deepest layer of periosteum and lining
the vascular canals of compact bone (endosteum).
Function: According to the function needed they divide by mitosis
to give any type of bone cells

Morphology: It resembles mesenchymal cell with pale
stained nucleus and little eosinophilic cytoplasm.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Osteoblasts
chunks.text:
Osteoblasts
§ Mononucleated cells are mesenchymal in origin found over the bone surface.
§ Cuboidal or flattened bone lining cells ( acc. to activity)
§ Synthesize the collagenous & non-collagenous bone matrix proteins.
§ Osteoid is an uncalcified bone matrix.
§ Show alkaline phosphatase activity (mineralization).
§ Have abundant protein synthetic cell organelles.
§ Gap junction are present between cells

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Osteocytes
chunks.text:
Osteocytes
§ Entrapped osteoblasts within its matrix they secrete.
§ The more rapid the bone formation , the more osteocytes.
§ The space of the cell is called lacunae.
§ The space of their osteocytic processes are called canaliculi.
§ Through these channels, the cells contact with each other and with osteoblasts.
§ Thus , maintain bone integrity and vitality.
§ They cannot divide.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Osteoclasts
chunks.text:
Osteoclasts
1. Large multinucleated cells which are hematopoietic .
2. The cell organelles are Golgi complex, mitochondria, RER & many
vesicles.
3. It has a vacuolated cytoplasm and a brush border adjacent to the
resorbing hard tissue.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Osteoclasts
chunks.text:
Osteoclasts
§ They are found in bay like depression of the resorbing bone that are called
Howship's lacunae reflecting the activity and mobility of the cells
during active resorption.
§ Electron microscope reveals a ruffled border consisting of deep
invaginations of the cell membrane forming numerous
intermingled villus like processes.
§Clear or sealing zone at the periphery of the this border that devoid of
organelles and enriched in proteins for adhesion (actin & myosin).

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Osteoclasts
chunks.text:
Osteoclasts
A proton pump is associated with the ruffled border that pumps hydrogen ions
into the sealed compartment for decalcification.
The osteoclasts are rich in acid phosphatase, collagenase & proteolytic
enzymes that degrade bone matrix.

chunks.title: Alveolar Bone
chunks.heading: Mechanism of bone resorption
chunks.text:
Mechanism of bone resorption
§ Attachment of osteoclast to the bone.
§ Creation of a sealed acidic microenvironment through the action of
proton pump to demineralize the bone & expose the organic
matrix.
§ Degradation of the organic matrix by the action of the released
enzymes (acid phosphatase, collagenase, proteolytic & cathepsin).
§ Endocytosis at the ruffled border of the organic products.
§ Release of the products along the membrane opposite the ruffled
border. (transcytosis).
